scenarios.title: The outage the CFO feared most
scenarios.situation: A regional distributor's order-processing system goes down for six hours during the holiday rush. Customer data is intact and was never exposed, but no orders ship. The CFO calls it the worst security incident of the year; the CISO says nothing was breached.
scenarios.prompt: Which leg of the CIA triad failed here, and what does that tell you about how to prioritize the fix?
choices: Confidentiality — order data sat unencrypted; prioritize encrypting the database first
Integrity — the orders were altered in transit; prioritize checksums on every transaction
Authentication — users could not log in, so the login system is the real failure
Availability — the system must stay reachable; prioritize redundancy and recovery over more encryption
scenarios.why: Confidentiality protects data from exposure, integrity protects it from tampering, and availability keeps systems usable. Nothing leaked and nothing was altered — orders simply could not flow, so availability is the failed leg. That points the fix at redundancy, failover, and tested recovery rather than more encryption.
scenarios.hint: Was any data seen by the wrong eyes, or changed? Or did the business just stop?

scenarios.title: Three controls walk into an audit
scenarios.situation: An auditor asks you to classify three controls at a clinic: (1) a written policy requiring unique logins, (2) badge readers on the server room door, (3) an annual phishing simulation for staff.
scenarios.prompt: Which classification is correct?
choices: Managerial, technical, operational — but all three are detective
Technical, managerial, operational — the policy is enforced by software
Managerial, technical, operational — the policy is managerial, the badge reader is technical, the training is operational
Operational, technical, managerial — in reverse order of cost
scenarios.why: Control families describe who owns them: managerial controls are policies and governance, technical controls are enforced by systems like badge readers and firewalls, and operational controls are carried out by people and processes like training. Knowing the family helps an auditor confirm every risk has an owner.
scenarios.hint: Ask who runs each control: a document, a device, or people doing a thing?

scenarios.title: The camera that could not stop anything
scenarios.situation: After a laptop theft, a manager says the cameras are preventive controls. The footage clearly shows the theft, but nobody was watching live and nothing blocked the thief.
scenarios.prompt: How do you correctly classify the camera system, and why does the distinction matter?
evidence: Incident note

Camera recorded the theft at 02:14.
No alert fired; guard reviewed footage the next morning.
choices: Preventive — cameras always deter; the theft proves staff need more training
Corrective — footage restores the laptop; classification does not matter
Detective — it records evidence after the fact; the distinction matters because detective controls need a response process to be useful
Compensating — cameras replace the missing guard; reclassify and move on
scenarios.why: Controls are also classified by function: preventive blocks, detective discovers, corrective restores, and compensating substitutes. A camera nobody monitors is detective at best — and a detective control without someone to respond to its findings is decoration. Match the function to the gap before buying more gear.
scenarios.hint: Did the camera stop the theft, catch it happening, or just remember it?

scenarios.title: The key-exchange problem
scenarios.situation: Two branch offices need to exchange encrypted backups nightly. The engineer proposes AES-256 with a single shared key emailed between the sites; the architect counters with RSA to exchange the AES key first.
scenarios.prompt: What is the real problem with the engineer's plan, and what does the architect's approach fix?
choices: Speed — AES is too slow for backups; RSA should encrypt everything instead
Key length — 256 bits is too short; the architect's plan uses longer keys
Compliance — email is banned; the fix is to use a phone call instead
Key distribution — emailing the shared secret exposes it; asymmetric encryption protects the key exchange while fast symmetric crypto moves the bulk data
scenarios.why: Symmetric encryption (AES) is fast, but both sides must somehow share the secret key — sending it over the channel you are trying to protect defeats the purpose. Asymmetric encryption (RSA) lets the sites exchange the AES session key safely: the public key encrypts, only the private key decrypts. This hybrid pattern is exactly how TLS works.
scenarios.hint: How does the secret key itself travel safely?

scenarios.title: The download that did not match
scenarios.situation: You download a vendor's firmware update. The vendor's site lists a SHA-256 hash, but your computed hash is completely different, though the filename and size look right.
scenarios.prompt: What does the mismatch tell you, and what is the correct next step?
evidence: Terminal

$ sha256sum firmware.bin
4a44dc15…c9e0  firmware.bin
Vendor published: 9f86d081…0f00a08
choices: SHA-256 is outdated — the mismatch is expected; install anyway
The file's integrity is broken — do not install it; re-download from the vendor's official source and investigate
The hash proves the file is malware — wipe the workstation immediately
Filenames match so it is fine — hashes are only advisory
scenarios.why: A cryptographic hash is a fingerprint: any change to the file, however small, produces a wildly different digest. A mismatch means the file is not the one the vendor published — corrupted or tampered with. Never install it; fetch a fresh copy over a trusted channel and find out what altered the first one.
scenarios.hint: What is a hash actually promising you?

scenarios.title: The browser's red warning
scenarios.situation: Staff report a red certificate-expired warning on the company intranet. The certificate expired yesterday; the private key is safe on the server, and the issuing CA is still trusted.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct remediation, and which PKI component must you protect most carefully during it?
choices: Delete the CA from trust stores; the CA is the problem
Tell users to click through the warning; expired certificates still encrypt
Renew or reissue the certificate from the CA and install it; guard the private key — anyone with it can impersonate the server
Generate a new key pair and email the private key to the CA for signing
scenarios.why: Expiry is routine: get a fresh certificate signed by your CA and install it. The critical asset is the private key — it never leaves the server and is never emailed. A certificate is public; the private key is what proves identity, so its compromise means reissuing everything.
scenarios.hint: Which part of the pair is public, and which must never travel?

scenarios.title: The signature nobody can deny
scenarios.situation: A supplier claims they never approved a $200,000 purchase order your system shows as approved. The approval was digitally signed with the supplier's private key.
scenarios.prompt: Why does the digital signature settle the dispute in a way a scanned handwritten signature would not?
choices: Encryption — the signature keeps the order secret from everyone
Speed — digital signatures are processed faster by the system
Non-repudiation — only the holder of the private key could have created it, and any alteration breaks the signature
Cost — digital signatures are free while ink costs money
scenarios.why: A digital signature is made by hashing the document and encrypting the hash with the signer's private key. Anyone can verify it with the public key, but only the private-key holder could have produced it — and tampering with the document invalidates the signature. That combination delivers non-repudiation: the signer cannot credibly deny it later.
scenarios.hint: What two things does the signature bind together: the signer and what else?

scenarios.title: Layered Defense for a Small Clinic
scenarios.situation: A 25-person medical clinic has one aging perimeter firewall and nothing else. Last month a receptionist opened a malicious attachment and ransomware encrypted two workstations before IT pulled the network cable. The owner has budget for exactly one security improvement this quarter.
scenarios.prompt: Which single investment gives the clinic the best defense-in-depth value for the money?
choices: Replace the firewall with a top-tier next-generation model
Deploy MFA on all accounts, automated offline backups, and a managed patching cadence
Buy an expensive EDR platform and install it on the two previously infected workstations only
Hire a part-time security guard to watch the server closet
scenarios.why: Defense in depth means layering independent controls so one failure doesn't equal compromise. MFA blocks credential theft, offline backups neutralize ransomware's leverage, and patching closes exploit paths — three layers covering identity, recovery, and prevention. A better firewall is still one layer at one point; the attack last month bypassed the perimeter entirely via email. Guards and partial EDR don't address the actual attack paths.
scenarios.hint: The attack came in through email, not through the firewall — where would independent layers have stopped it?
objectives: Compare control categories by attack path
evidence: Selected a layered control set that addresses the actual email-borne attack path

scenarios.title: The invoice from your CFO
scenarios.situation: Accounts payable gets an email that looks like it is from the CFO: same display name, an urgent wire transfer for an acquisition, and a reply-to going to a lookalike domain. The real CFO is on a flight.
scenarios.prompt: What is this attack, and what is the single most effective verification step?
evidence: Email headers (excerpt)

From: "CFO" <cfo@acrne-corp.com>
Reply-To: cfo@acrne-corp.com
Subject: URGENT: wire needed before market open
choices: Spear phishing — verify out-of-band by calling the CFO on a known number before moving any money
A worm — disconnect the mail server immediately
Ransomware — the attachment will encrypt the AP workstation
A DDoS — the urgency is meant to flood the AP team
scenarios.why: Spear phishing targets specific people with researched, convincing lures — here, a lookalike domain and a timely pretext. The defense is procedural, not just technical: any payment instruction arriving by email gets verified through a separate trusted channel before funds move. No filter catches everything, so the callback rule is the real control.
scenarios.hint: The email is the weapon; what channel did the attacker not compromise?

scenarios.title: The IT help desk that called you
scenarios.situation: An employee gets a call from IT support about suspicious account activity. The caller knows the employee's name and manager, and asks them to read back the MFA code just texted to their phone to verify identity.
scenarios.prompt: What is happening, and what should the employee do?
choices: Legitimate support — read the code; IT needs it to secure the account
A wrong number — ignore it and change nothing
Smishing — reply STOP to the text message
Vishing — hang up and call the real help desk on the published number; never read an MFA code to an inbound caller
scenarios.why: Voice phishing (vishing) uses personal details — often from LinkedIn or prior breaches — to sound legitimate, then steals the MFA code to hijack the session. Real IT will never ask for your MFA code; the code proves possession to the system, and handing it to a caller hands them your session. Hang up and verify via a known number.
scenarios.hint: Who initiated this contact, and what does the MFA code actually prove?

scenarios.title: The login box that logged everyone in
scenarios.situation: A tester types a single quote followed by OR '1'='1 into the username field of an old internal app and is instantly logged in as the first user in the database. The query log shows the input was concatenated straight into SQL.
scenarios.prompt: What is the vulnerability, and what is the correct fix?
evidence: App log
SELECT * FROM users WHERE name='' OR '1'='1' --' AND pass='...'
choices: SQL injection — use parameterized queries so input is never treated as code
Cross-site scripting — escape HTML output on the login page
CSRF — add tokens to the login form
Broken authentication — require longer passwords
scenarios.why: When user input is glued into a SQL string, the database cannot tell data from commands — the injected logic rewrites the query itself. Parameterized queries send the code and the data separately, so input is always treated as a value. Input validation helps, but parameterization is the structural fix.
scenarios.hint: Where exactly does the attacker's text end up — as data, or as part of the command?

scenarios.title: The support ticket that ran code
scenarios.situation: A customer submits a support ticket containing a script tag that sends the viewer's session cookie to an external server. When an agent opens the ticket, their session cookie is exfiltrated.
scenarios.prompt: What is this attack, and what two defenses break the chain?
choices: SQL injection — parameterize the ticket database queries
Phishing — train agents not to open tickets from strangers
Ransomware — the script will encrypt the agent's workstation
Stored XSS — encode output when rendering user content, and set cookies HttpOnly so scripts cannot read them
scenarios.why: Stored cross-site scripting persists the attacker's script in the application — here, a ticket — so it executes in every victim's browser. Output encoding neutralizes the script at render time, and the HttpOnly cookie flag keeps JavaScript from reading session cookies: defense in depth on both ends of the chain.
scenarios.hint: Where does the script live, and whose browser runs it?

scenarios.title: The ransom note on the file server
scenarios.situation: Monday 6 AM: the file server shows a ransom note, shares are encrypted, and the wallpaper changed on fifty workstations. The note demands payment within 72 hours. Backups exist but were last tested six months ago.
scenarios.prompt: What are the correct first actions, in order?
choices: Pay immediately to beat the deadline, then investigate
Isolate affected systems from the network, then begin incident response — do not pay before exhausting recovery options
Wipe and rebuild everything at once to save time
Delete the ransom note so staff do not panic
scenarios.why: Containment comes first: disconnect affected hosts so the ransomware cannot reach backups or spread further. Then work the incident response plan — assess scope, attempt recovery from backups, involve leadership and legal. Paying funds criminals, rarely guarantees decryption, and may be legally restricted.
scenarios.hint: What is still spreading while you are reading the note?

scenarios.title: The scan that found everything and proved nothing
scenarios.situation: A quarterly vulnerability scan flags 400 findings, mostly missing patches. Leadership asks whether the company is actually exploitable. The security team debates ordering a penetration test.
scenarios.prompt: What is the key difference the team should explain to leadership?
choices: Scanning finds potential weaknesses automatically; penetration testing has humans attempt controlled exploitation to prove real-world impact
They are the same thing — the scan already proves exploitability
Penetration tests are fully automated and cheaper than scans
Scans are illegal without a warrant; pen tests are not
scenarios.why: Vulnerability scanning is broad, automated, and safe — it lists what might be wrong. A penetration test is narrow, human-driven, and scoped: testers chain weaknesses together to demonstrate actual business impact, with rules of engagement to avoid damage. Leadership gets prioritization from the scan and proof of impact from the test.
scenarios.hint: Which one answers whether an attacker could actually get in through this?

scenarios.title: The logins that came from everywhere
scenarios.situation: Overnight, the VPN gateway logged one failed login per account across 300 accounts — each tried once with the same seasonal password. No account was locked out.
scenarios.prompt: What is this attack, and which control most directly blunts it?
evidence: VPN log (excerpt)

03:12:01 failed login: j.smith from 185.220.x.x
03:12:44 failed login: a.jones from 185.220.x.x
... 298 more, one attempt each
choices: A brute-force attack on one account — lock the targeted account
Credential stuffing with unique passwords — force a password reset for all users
Password spraying — enforce MFA so a guessed password alone is useless
A DDoS attack — add more VPN capacity
scenarios.why: Password spraying flips brute force sideways: one common password against many accounts, staying under per-account lockout thresholds. Because lockouts will not trigger, the effective defense is MFA — a correct password alone no longer grants access — plus alerting on distributed low-and-slow patterns.
scenarios.hint: Why did no account lock out?

scenarios.title: The Urgent Call from 'IT'
scenarios.situation: A finance clerk receives a call from someone claiming to be from the company's IT security team. The caller knows her name and manager's name, says her workstation is beaconing to a known malicious server, and urgently needs her to install a 'diagnostic tool' from a link he texts her. She is about to click.
scenarios.prompt: What is the most effective control against this specific attack?
choices: A stronger email spam filter
Endpoint antivirus with real-time protection
A verification procedure: hang up, call the IT help desk on the published internal number, and confirm before acting
Blocking all text-message links on company phones
scenarios.why: This is vishing — voice phishing, a social engineering attack that exploits authority and urgency, not a technical vulnerability. Technical controls can't reliably stop a willing user from installing attacker software, but an out-of-band verification procedure breaks the attacker's core leverage: impersonated authority. Spam filters and AV don't address phone-based social engineering, and blocking SMS links treats a symptom while the same con works over a voice call.
scenarios.hint: The attacker's weapon is persuasion over the phone, not malware delivery through a technical channel.
objectives: Select human-layer controls for social attacks
evidence: Chose out-of-band verification as the control against a vishing attack

scenarios.title: The VPN that trusted too much
scenarios.situation: An attacker phished one VPN credential and moved freely across the flat corporate network for weeks — finance servers, backups, everything — because being inside the VPN meant being trusted.
scenarios.prompt: Which Zero Trust principle most directly addresses this failure?
choices: Never trust, always verify — authenticate and authorize every access request based on identity and context, and segment so a foothold does not mean the kingdom
Trust but verify — the VPN just needed a longer password
Perimeter defense — build a taller firewall around the VPN
Air gap everything — disconnect the network entirely
scenarios.why: Zero Trust assumes breach and removes implicit trust: every request is verified by identity, device health, and context, and access is least-privilege and segmented. The VPN failure was architectural — one credential bought the whole network. Microsegmentation and identity-aware access shrink what any single compromise can reach.
scenarios.hint: What did the attacker get for free after the first login?

scenarios.title: The worm that walked the flat network
scenarios.situation: A worm entered through an unpatched print server and reached every workstation and server in the building within an hour. There are no internal firewalls — one broadcast domain everywhere.
scenarios.prompt: What architectural change contains the next worm, and why?
choices: Buy faster switches so the worm spreads more slowly
Put everything in one bigger subnet for easier monitoring
Remove the print server; peripherals do not need security
Segment the network with VLANs and firewall zones so lateral movement hits boundaries — containment is about limiting blast radius
scenarios.why: Segmentation divides the network into zones with controlled crossings, so a compromise in one zone cannot freely reach the others. VLANs plus firewall rules between zones turn a flat freeway into gated neighborhoods. It is the architectural answer to lateral movement.
scenarios.hint: The worm moved sideways — what would have been in its way?

scenarios.title: The unpatched server in the cloud
scenarios.situation: A company runs its app on EC2 instances (IaaS). A breach traces to an unpatched OS vulnerability. The CTO says they thought the cloud provider handled patching.
scenarios.prompt: Who was actually responsible for patching the guest OS, and why?
evidence: Architecture note

Compute: EC2 instances (customer-managed AMIs)
Provider manages: facilities, hypervisor, physical network
choices: The customer — under shared responsibility, the provider secures the cloud itself while the customer secures what they put in it, including the guest OS on IaaS
The provider — cloud means they patch everything
Nobody — patching is optional on IaaS
The auditor — findings assign responsibility
scenarios.why: Shared responsibility splits at the service line: the provider owns security of the cloud (physical, hypervisor, facilities); the customer owns security in the cloud. On IaaS that includes the guest OS, patching, and firewall rules. Managed services shift more upward — but the data and access always stay with the customer.
scenarios.hint: Who chose and configured the operating system?

scenarios.title: The team that did not want servers
scenarios.situation: A five-person startup needs a customer database and a web app. They have no operations staff and no appetite for patching operating systems — they just want to write code and store data.
scenarios.prompt: Which cloud model fits best, and why?
choices: IaaS — maximum control is always best for startups
On-premises — the cloud is never appropriate for databases
Bare-metal colocation — they should rack their own servers
PaaS and managed services — the provider manages the OS and runtime; the team focuses on code and data with minimal operational burden
scenarios.why: Cloud models trade control for operational burden: IaaS gives you VMs you must manage, PaaS gives you a platform where the provider handles the OS and runtime, SaaS gives you finished software. A tiny team with no ops capacity should climb the stack — PaaS for the app, a managed database — and spend their hours on the product.
scenarios.hint: Who patches the OS in each model?

scenarios.title: The backup that saved the quarter
scenarios.situation: Ransomware encrypted the primary file shares and — because the backup drive was mapped on the same network — the online backups too. The one thing that survived was a monthly offline copy in a safe.
scenarios.prompt: What backup principle does this prove, and what should change?
evidence: Backup report

Nightly backup: network share (encrypted by ransomware)
Monthly offline copy: intact, 28 days old
choices: Backups are useless — 28 days of data loss is unacceptable, so stop backing up
3-2-1 with offline copies — keep three copies on two media types with one off-site or offline; backups reachable from production are not really backups
Encrypt the backups with the same key as production for simplicity
Back up less often to save disk space
scenarios.why: The 3-2-1 rule — three copies, two different media, one off-site — exists precisely because ransomware hunts reachable backups. An air-gapped or immutable copy the malware cannot touch is the difference between a bad month and a dead company. Also: test restores regularly, or the backup is a rumor.
scenarios.hint: Why did the offline copy survive when the network one did not?

scenarios.title: The firewall that was the business
scenarios.situation: The company's single internet firewall dies on a Friday night. No failover, no spare — the business is offline until Monday because the firewall was a single point of failure.
scenarios.prompt: What resilience pattern prevents a repeat?
choices: A bigger firewall — size prevents failure
More bandwidth — outages are always capacity problems
High availability with redundant components and failover — eliminate single points of failure on critical paths
A faster ISP — the firewall was not the issue
scenarios.why: Resilience is designed: redundant components, automatic failover, and tested recovery plans remove single points of failure. Bigger boxes still fail — pairs of boxes with failover keep the business up. Identify what is critical, duplicate it, and prove the failover works before you need it.
scenarios.hint: What was the one thing with no backup?

scenarios.title: The credentials in cleartext
scenarios.situation: A packet capture on the office network shows usernames and passwords in plain text. Investigation finds admins still use Telnet to manage switches and FTP for config backups.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct remediation?
choices: Add a firewall; cleartext protocols are fine behind one
Replace Telnet with SSH and FTP with SFTP or SCP — encrypt management traffic so credentials cannot be sniffed
Change the passwords more often; the protocols are fine
Capture fewer packets so nobody notices
scenarios.why: Telnet (port 23) and FTP (ports 20/21) transmit everything — including credentials — in cleartext; anyone on the path can read them. SSH (port 22) and SFTP/SCP encrypt the session. Legacy protocols persist because they still work, but on any network you do not fully control, they are credential donors.
scenarios.hint: What does an eavesdropper see with each protocol?

scenarios.title: Segmenting the Smart Hospital Wing
scenarios.situation: A hospital wing just deployed 200 IoT devices — infusion pumps, smart thermostats, badge readers — that only the vendor can patch, and several run firmware with known vulnerabilities. They currently sit on the same flat network as nurse workstations and the billing system.
scenarios.prompt: What architecture change best reduces risk from these unpatchable devices?
choices: Give every IoT device a public IP so the vendor can reach them directly for support
Move the IoT devices to an isolated VLAN/segment with strict ACLs allowing only required vendor and monitoring traffic
Install host antivirus on each IoT device
Require nurses to use VPN when accessing the billing system
scenarios.why: Segmentation contains the blast radius: devices that cannot be hardened get network-level containment instead. A dedicated VLAN with deny-by-default ACLs limits lateral movement so a compromised thermostat can't reach billing systems or workstations, while still permitting the few flows the devices genuinely need. Public IPs expand exposure; host AV isn't installable on embedded firmware; nurse VPN does nothing about device-to-device lateral movement on the flat LAN.
scenarios.hint: When you can't fix the endpoint, contain it with the network — what's the network-layer way to isolate?
evidence: Designed an isolated segment with ACLs to contain vulnerable IoT devices

scenarios.title: The alerts that meant something together
scenarios.situation: The SIEM fires three low-severity alerts within ten minutes: a user VPNs in from an unusual country, reads an odd volume from the file share, then emails a large attachment externally. Each alert alone is routine.
scenarios.prompt: What is the SIEM doing that a human watching one log could not, and what is the right next step?
evidence: SIEM timeline

09:02 VPN login — new geolocation (low)
09:07 file share: 4.2 GB read (low)
09:11 outbound email: 3.8 GB attachment (low)
Correlation rule EXFIL-PATTERN → critical
choices: Generating false positives — close all three as noise
Blocking the user automatically — the SIEM has already handled it
Reinstalling the VPN client — the geolocation is a glitch
Correlating events across sources into one high-fidelity alert — escalate and investigate as potential data exfiltration
scenarios.why: A SIEM's power is correlation: joining weak signals from different sources into a pattern no single log reveals. Three low events in sequence match an exfiltration playbook, so the correlation rule raises it to critical. The analyst's job now is investigation — verify, contain, and determine scope — not dismissal.
scenarios.hint: What story do the three events tell in order?

scenarios.title: The log file that confessed
scenarios.situation: Users report the SSH bastion feels slow. You open /var/log/auth.log and see thousands of Failed password lines from two IP addresses, cycling through usernames like admin, root, and test.
scenarios.prompt: What is happening, and what are the two immediate actions?
evidence: auth.log (excerpt)

Failed password for root from 203.0.113.44
Failed password for admin from 203.0.113.44
Failed password for test from 203.0.113.78
... (4,200 similar lines)
choices: Normal traffic — SSH always logs failures; ignore it
A misconfigured monitoring tool — whitelist the IPs permanently
Brute-force attack — block the source IPs at the firewall and enforce key-based auth or disable password SSH
Disk full — rotate the logs and move on
scenarios.why: Thousands of failed logins from a few IPs cycling common usernames is a brute-force attack against SSH. Immediate moves: block the attackers at the perimeter and reduce the attack surface — key-based authentication, or disabling password auth, makes guessing infeasible.
scenarios.hint: Would legitimate users fail thousands of times from the same two addresses?

scenarios.title: The urge to wipe it clean
scenarios.situation: A workstation shows ransomware behavior. A well-meaning technician wants to immediately reimage it to get the user working again. The incident response lead stops them.
scenarios.prompt: Why is the lead right, and which incident response phase comes before eradication?
choices: The lead is wrong — speed of recovery is all that matters
Preparation comes after eradication in the lifecycle
Containment and evidence preservation come first — wiping destroys forensic evidence and may not stop the spread; eradication follows containment
Wiping is containment; the technician was correct
scenarios.why: The incident response lifecycle runs preparation, then detection and analysis, containment, eradication, recovery, and lessons learned. Jumping to eradication (wiping) before containment lets the threat keep spreading and destroys evidence needed to find the root cause. Discipline in the order is what separates response from panic.
scenarios.hint: If you wipe the machine, what questions can you never answer?

scenarios.title: The memory that forgets first
scenarios.situation: A server is suspected of running in-memory-only malware. The analyst debates what to collect first: the RAM contents, the disk image, or the system logs.
scenarios.prompt: What does the order of volatility dictate?
choices: Image the disk first — it is the biggest evidence source
Collect RAM first — memory is the most volatile; disk and logs persist longer and can wait
Read the logs first — they are the easiest
Power off immediately — volatility does not matter
scenarios.why: Order of volatility says collect the most ephemeral evidence first: CPU registers and RAM, then network state, then disk, then logs and archives. In-memory malware lives only in RAM — reboot or delay and it is gone forever. Disk images and logs will still be there after the memory capture.
scenarios.hint: Which evidence disappears if the machine reboots?

scenarios.title: The USB drive in the evidence bag
scenarios.situation: An employee's USB drive is suspected of carrying stolen designs. The manager wants to plug it into their own laptop just to see what is on it.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct handling, and why?
choices: Bag, tag, hash, and document every handler — chain of custody proves the evidence was not altered; plugging it in anywhere destroys that proof
Plug it into any machine — curiosity is fine if you do not change files
Format it to remove the malware risk, then investigate
Mail it to the employee's home for safekeeping
scenarios.why: Chain of custody is the documented trail of who handled evidence, when, and what they did — it is what makes evidence admissible and trustworthy. Hashing at seizure proves later that nothing changed. Every undocumented touch, even a well-meaning peek, breaks the chain and can sink an investigation or legal case.
scenarios.hint: If this ends up in court, what will the other side ask about the drive?

scenarios.title: The 400 findings and the one weekend
scenarios.situation: A scan returns 400 vulnerabilities. The team can patch about 30 systems this weekend. Two critical CVSS 9.8 findings sit on an isolated test server; a CVSS 7.5 sits on the internet-facing payment portal.
scenarios.prompt: How should the team prioritize?
choices: Strictly by CVSS score — patch the 9.8s first no matter what
Risk-based: weigh severity together with asset criticality and exposure — the internet-facing 7.5 likely outranks the isolated 9.8s
Alphabetically by hostname, for fairness
Patch whatever is fastest to maximize the count
scenarios.why: CVSS measures the vulnerability's severity, not your risk. Risk adds context: asset value, exposure, existing controls, and threat activity. A medium bug on the payment portal facing the internet is more dangerous than a critical bug on an isolated lab box. Prioritize by risk, not by score alone.
scenarios.hint: Which system would an attacker actually reach first?

scenarios.title: The server that should never be touched
scenarios.situation: The SOC deploys a server that mimics the finance database but holds fake data and has no legitimate users. Any login attempt to it pages the on-call analyst.
scenarios.prompt: What is this, and what value does it provide?
choices: A backup server — it protects finance data
A load balancer — it distributes finance queries
A firewall — it blocks finance traffic
A honeypot — any interaction is malicious by definition, giving high-fidelity detection and attacker intelligence
scenarios.why: A honeypot is a decoy with no production purpose, so every touch is suspicious — that makes its alerts extremely high-fidelity compared to noisy IDS signatures. It also wastes attacker time and reveals their tools and techniques. The trade-off: it must be isolated so a compromise cannot pivot into real systems.
scenarios.hint: If nobody legitimate should ever touch it, what does a touch mean?

scenarios.title: The Friday-Afternoon Critical Patch
scenarios.situation: At 3 PM on a Friday, the vendor publishes a critical remote-code-execution patch for the VPN concentrator that all remote staff use. Active exploitation is reported in the wild. The normal change window is Sunday 2 AM, and the change advisory board won't meet until Monday.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct operational response?
choices: Wait for the Sunday window and the Monday CAB meeting — process must be followed
Have an engineer patch it immediately with no documentation to save time
Invoke the emergency change process: assess, get expedited approval, patch, and document everything
Disable the VPN entirely until Monday and tell staff to come to the office
scenarios.why: Operations security balances speed and control through the emergency change process — it exists precisely for critical, actively-exploited vulnerabilities where waiting invites compromise. It preserves the key safeguards (impact assessment, approval, rollback plan, documentation) while compressing the timeline. Skipping process entirely removes accountability and rollback safety; waiting leaves a known-exploited remote entry point open all weekend; killing the VPN is a disproportionate availability hit when a controlled emergency patch is available.
scenarios.hint: There's a formal process designed exactly for 'patch now, but stay controlled' — which option uses it?
objectives: Balance availability vs security under active exploitation
evidence: Selected the emergency change process for an actively exploited critical vulnerability

scenarios.title: The risk nobody wanted to own
scenarios.situation: The risk register lists unencrypted customer database backups as high risk. Engineering says fixing it costs $40,000; the business says a breach would cost roughly $2,000,000 and is unlikely but possible. Nobody will sign as risk owner.
scenarios.prompt: What is the missing governance step, and what are the legitimate response options?
choices: Delete the register entry so auditors do not see it
Assign an owner and choose: mitigate, transfer (insurance), accept (formally, with sign-off), or avoid — but ignore is not an option
Accept the risk verbally with no documentation
Buy insurance and skip the encryption work entirely
scenarios.why: Risk management requires an owner and a documented decision: mitigate (fix it), transfer (insurance and contracts), accept (conscious sign-off at the right level), or avoid (stop the activity). An unsigned, unowned risk is just a future incident. Insurance transfers financial impact — it does not remove the duty to protect data.
scenarios.hint: Who gets to say we are fine with this — and where is that written down?

scenarios.title: The control that cost more than the risk
scenarios.situation: A $200,000 server has a vulnerability with an exposure factor of 25% and an expected occurrence rate of once every 4 years. A vendor quotes $18,000 per year for a control that fully prevents it.
scenarios.prompt: What is the annualized loss expectancy, and what does it say about the purchase?
evidence: Risk worksheet

Asset value: $200,000
Exposure factor: 25%
Annualized rate of occurrence: 0.25
choices: ALE is $12,500 per year — the $18,000 control costs more than the risk it removes; consider cheaper mitigations or formal acceptance
ALE is $50,000 per year — buy the control immediately
ALE is $200,000 per year — the server must be decommissioned
Math does not apply to security — buy every control offered
scenarios.why: Quantitative risk uses SLE = asset value x exposure factor ($50,000) and ALE = SLE x ARO ($50,000 x 0.25 = $12,500). A control should cost less than the risk it mitigates — otherwise you are spending $18,000 to save $12,500. Numbers do not decide alone, but they stop fear-based buying.
scenarios.hint: Work it stepwise: single loss first, then annualize.

scenarios.title: The document that was not a policy
scenarios.situation: An auditor asks for the access-control policy. The team hands over a 40-page step-by-step guide for creating accounts in Active Directory. The auditor says that is a procedure and asks where the policy is.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct hierarchy, and what belongs at each level?
choices: Policy states the what and why (management intent), standards set mandatory rules, procedures give step-by-step how — the team produced the bottom layer only
Procedures outrank policies; the auditor is wrong
Policies must be 40+ pages; shorter documents are procedures
There is no hierarchy — any document counts as policy
scenarios.why: Governance flows downward: policies state management's intent and direction, standards and baselines set mandatory specifics, procedures document the exact steps, and guidelines offer recommendations. Auditors test whether practice matches the policy chain — a procedure without a parent policy is an orphan with no authority.
scenarios.hint: Which document would a CEO sign, and which would a technician follow at 2 AM?

scenarios.title: The vendor with the keys to everything
scenarios.situation: A payroll vendor will hold all employee PII and needs VPN access into the HR network. Their sales rep says they are very secure but provides no audit reports.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct third-party risk process before signing?
choices: Sign immediately — sales reps are vetted by their own company
Skip review for payroll; only software vendors need assessment
Give them domain admin to simplify the integration
Due diligence: security questionnaire, SOC 2 report review, contract terms (right to audit, breach notification, data return), and least-privilege access — trust is verified, not assumed
scenarios.why: Third-party risk management treats vendors as an extension of your attack surface: assess their controls (questionnaires, SOC 2 Type II reports), bind them contractually (breach notification timelines, audit rights, data handling and return), and grant minimum necessary access with monitoring. Trust us is not a control.
scenarios.hint: If they get breached, whose employees' data is on the news?

scenarios.title: The alphabet soup of compliance
scenarios.situation: A retailer expands into the EU and starts storing cardholder data. Legal asks which frameworks apply: the team debates GDPR, PCI-DSS, and HIPAA.
scenarios.prompt: Which applies and why?
choices: Only HIPAA — it covers all personal data everywhere
GDPR (EU personal data) and PCI-DSS (cardholder data) apply; HIPAA covers health information and does not fit a retailer
None — compliance is voluntary for retailers
GDPR only — PCI-DSS was replaced by GDPR
scenarios.why: Compliance follows the data: GDPR governs personal data of EU individuals, PCI-DSS governs anyone storing or processing cardholder data, HIPAA governs protected health information in healthcare. Know what data you hold and where your customers are — that determines your obligations, not your industry label.
scenarios.hint: Match each regulation to the data type it protects.

scenarios.title: The phishing test with a 40% click rate
scenarios.situation: The first company-wide phishing simulation gets a 40% click rate and 15% credential submission. Leadership wants to punish the clickers; the security team proposes something else.
scenarios.prompt: What is the effective security-awareness response?
choices: Targeted retraining and repeated simulations to drive the rate down — awareness is measured by behavior change, not punishment
Public shaming of the 40% — fear works best
Fire repeat clickers immediately
Stop the simulations — they make the metrics look bad
scenarios.why: Awareness programs exist to change behavior: baseline with a simulation, train (especially the clickers), re-simulate, and track the trend. Punishment drives reporting underground — you want users who report suspicious mail, not users who hide their mistakes. The metric that matters is the click rate going down and the report rate going up.
scenarios.hint: Do you want employees who fear the test, or employees who report the phish?

scenarios.title: The system that could not wait
scenarios.situation: The business impact analysis asks each department how long systems can be down. Order processing says four hours or they lose the day's revenue; the archival document system says two weeks is fine.
scenarios.prompt: What are these values, and how do they drive recovery planning?
choices: They are SLAs — the IT team must guarantee them to customers
They are RPO only — time does not matter, only data loss
BIA is a technical exercise — business input is irrelevant
Recovery Time Objective (RTO) and Recovery Point Objective (RPO) per system — critical systems get faster, costlier recovery tiers; archives get the cheap tier
scenarios.why: The BIA quantifies impact to set RTO (how fast must it be back) and RPO (how much data loss is tolerable) per system. Those numbers drive disaster recovery investment: the four-hour order system earns redundant infrastructure and frequent backups; the archive earns a weekly tape. Recovery spending follows business impact, not IT preference.
scenarios.hint: Which number is about time, and which is about data?

scenarios.title: The Risk the Board Must Own
scenarios.situation: A penetration test found the company's legacy order-entry system has unfixable vulnerabilities, but replacing it costs $2M and the business can't operate without it. The security team estimates a 10% annual chance of a breach costing $500K. Leadership asks for a recommendation.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct governance recommendation?
choices: Accept the risk: document it, apply compensating controls, and get formal sign-off from senior leadership
Quietly ignore the finding since the system can't be replaced anyway
Have the security analyst sign the risk acceptance on behalf of the company
Buy a $50K firewall and declare the risk mitigated
scenarios.why: Risk acceptance is a legitimate strategy, but governance requires it to be explicit, documented, owned at the right level, and paired with compensating controls (monitoring, segmentation, backups) that reduce likelihood or impact. A $50K expected annual loss ($500K x 10%) may rationally be cheaper than a $2M replacement — but only senior leadership can own that business decision, never the analyst, and never silently. Declaring a firewall 'mitigates' unfixable app flaws misrepresents residual risk to decision-makers.
scenarios.hint: Risk acceptance is valid — but who must own it, and what must accompany it?
objectives: Identify proper risk ownership and documentation
evidence: Recommended documented risk acceptance with compensating controls and executive sign-off

domains.name: Systems Anatomy: Seeing Systems as Living Flows
domains.description: Learn to see Comptia Security Plus as living systems — not static diagrams, but moving sequences where every part connects. Master systems thinking for exams and interviews.

scenarios.title: The General Security Concepts Mystery
scenarios.situation: Users report that General Security Concepts is not working correctly. The obvious checks pass — the components are online, basic connectivity works. You need to think in systems, not symptoms.
scenarios.prompt: Using the systems anatomy method (whole → cut open → step through → pull apart), how would you systematically trace a failure in General Security Concepts?
choices: Walk the full journey: start from the trigger, verify each handoff in sequence, check dependencies at every step, and isolate where the flow breaks — then examine that specific layer
Restart all components — General Security Concepts issues are always fixed by restarting
Check the most common cause from memory and apply that fix immediately
Escalate to senior support — General Security Concepts is too complex to troubleshoot systematically
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Systems thinking means tracing the living flow: (1) Whole: what is General Security Concepts supposed to do end-to-end? (2) Cut open: what are the layers/stages? (3) Step through: verify each handoff — where does the expected output diverge from actual? (4) Pull apart: isolate the broken layer and examine it in detail. This method works for any General Security Concepts failure in Comptia Security Plus.
scenarios.hint: Don't jump to the fix. First map the journey, then find where it breaks.
objectives: Apply systems anatomy to General Security Concepts
evidence: System Status
All General Security Concepts components report 'online'. Basic health checks pass.
User Report
Functionality is broken despite green status indicators. The failure is in the flow, not the components.

scenarios.title: Kerberos: Where the Ticket Breaks
scenarios.situation: Users in a branch office suddenly can't access any file shares. They can log in to their workstations, ping the file server, and resolve its name — but every share access fails with an authentication error. The branch's link to headquarters, where the domain controllers live, went down 30 minutes ago and just came back up.
scenarios.prompt: Walking the Kerberos flow as a system, where is the failure?
choices: The file server's disk — authentication errors mean the data is unreachable
The client can't reach a KDC to get a service ticket, so it has no valid ticket to present to the file server
DNS is broken, so the workstation can't find the file server
The user's password expired during the outage
scenarios.why: Kerberos is a ticket-based journey: the client first contacts the KDC (AS exchange for a TGT, then TGS exchange for a service ticket) and only then presents the service ticket to the file server. Login worked because cached credentials allow local logon, and ping/DNS work because those don't need Kerberos — but every new service ticket request fails without KDC reachability. The system view pinpoints the break at the ticket-granting step, not at the server or the password.
scenarios.hint: Trace the journey: before the client ever talks to the file server, who must it talk to first?
evidence: Located an authentication failure at the KDC ticket-granting step of the Kerberos flow

scenarios.title: Packet Journey Through the Firewall
scenarios.situation: A web server in the DMZ needs to pull updates from the internet, and internal users need to reach it on HTTPS. The firewall admin wrote the rules top-down: (1) deny all, (2) allow internal-to-DMZ 443, (3) allow DMZ-to-internet 80/443. Return traffic for the update downloads is being dropped.
scenarios.prompt: Following the packet's journey through the firewall as a system, what is wrong?
choices: Rule 3's ports are wrong — updates need port 22
The deny-all rule is first, so nothing below it is ever evaluated
The firewall has no stateful inspection handling, so return traffic has no matching allow rule
The DMZ server needs a public IP address
scenarios.why: A firewall processes each packet as a journey: ingress interface → rule evaluation top-down → state table check → NAT → egress. Stateful inspection automatically permits return traffic for established sessions, but if this firewall is evaluating statelessly (or the state engine isn't engaged), the inbound SYN-ACK from the update server hits the rule base as a new connection and dies at 'deny all'. The fix is stateful handling (or explicit return rules), not port or addressing changes — and rule order matters, but 'deny all' belongs at the END, while here the scenario states it's listed first as the design, which combined with no statefulness kills return traffic.
scenarios.hint: The outbound SYN leaves fine, but the reply SYN-ACK arrives as a stranger — what firewall feature normally recognizes it?
objectives: Trace packet flow through firewall processing
Apply stateful inspection and rule-order logic
evidence: Diagnosed dropped return traffic as a stateful-inspection gap in the firewall packet journey

scenarios.title: VPN Tunnel Anatomy: Phase 1 Up, Phase 2 Down
scenarios.situation: A site-to-site IPsec VPN between headquarters and a new branch shows Phase 1 (IKE) as established, but no traffic passes and Phase 2 never completes. Both sides insist their configuration is correct. The branch admin mentions they 'hardened' their crypto settings last week.
scenarios.prompt: As a system, where do you look first?
choices: The physical WAN link — Phase 1 must be a false positive
Compare Phase 2 proposals: encryption, integrity, DH group, and lifetimes must match on both sides
Reboot both VPN gateways to clear the SA table
Increase the Phase 1 lifetime so the tunnel stays up longer
scenarios.why: An IPsec tunnel is a two-phase system: Phase 1 (IKE) builds the secure management channel, Phase 2 (IPsec SAs) negotiates the actual data-protection parameters. Phase 1 succeeding proves connectivity and peer authentication work — the break is inside the Phase 2 negotiation, where mismatched proposals (AES-256 vs AES-128, SHA-256 vs SHA-1, DH group, lifetimes, or proxy IDs/traffic selectors) cause the negotiation to fail. The branch's 'hardening' very likely changed one side's proposal set. Reboots and lifetimes don't fix a parameter mismatch.
scenarios.hint: Phase 1 is the handshake about HOW to talk securely; Phase 2 negotiates the actual data protection — which negotiation is failing, and what must both sides agree on?
evidence: Isolated a VPN failure to mismatched Phase 2 proposals after successful Phase 1

scenarios.title: DNS Resolution Chain: The Poisoned Step
scenarios.situation: Employees report that the company's banking portal intermittently loads a convincing fake login page. The real site's certificate is valid and the bank confirms no compromise. Internal DNS servers forward to the ISP resolver, and the fake page appears for about an hour at a time, then disappears.
scenarios.prompt: Walking the DNS resolution chain, what best explains the symptom?
choices: The bank's authoritative DNS server was hacked permanently
A cache-poisoning attack on a resolver in the chain injected a bogus record with a TTL of about an hour
Employees' browsers have a malicious extension rewriting the page
The company's firewall is redirecting HTTPS traffic
scenarios.why: DNS resolution is a chain: client → local resolver → (forwarders) → root → TLD → authoritative, with caching at each hop. Cache poisoning injects a forged answer into one resolver's cache, and the lie persists exactly until the record's TTL expires — matching the 'about an hour, then disappears' pattern. A hacked authoritative server wouldn't self-heal hourly; a browser extension wouldn't be intermittent across many users; and a firewall redirect would break the valid certificate (TLS would warn). The TTL-bound intermittence is the signature of a poisoned cache entry aging out.
scenarios.hint: What DNS mechanism makes a lie temporary — lasting a fixed time, then vanishing on its own?
objectives: Recognize cache-poisoning symptoms and TTL behavior
evidence: Attributed intermittent DNS redirection to cache poisoning via TTL-bound symptom analysis

scenarios.title: SOC Alert Pipeline: From Log to Analyst
scenarios.situation: A SOC manager complains analysts are drowning: 40,000 alerts a day, most never reviewed. The pipeline is: endpoints/servers forward logs → SIEM ingests → correlation rules fire → every rule hit creates a ticket → analysts work the queue oldest-first.
scenarios.prompt: Where is the highest-leverage fix in this pipeline as a system?
choices: Hire more analysts to work the queue faster
Tune and tier the pipeline: suppress known-benign patterns, deduplicate, enrich with asset/threat intel, and risk-score before ticket creation
Forward more log sources into the SIEM for better visibility
Work the queue newest-first instead of oldest-first
scenarios.why: The pipeline's bottleneck isn't analyst speed — it's that raw rule hits flow straight to humans with no signal processing. The highest-leverage fix sits between detection and ticketing: tuning out false positives, deduplicating repeat hits, enriching with context (is this a crown-jewel server? does threat intel flag the IOC?), and risk-scoring so analysts see the 200 alerts that matter instead of 40,000 undifferentiated ones. More analysts or more logs just scale the noise; queue order doesn't change the signal-to-noise ratio.
scenarios.hint: 40,000 tickets a day means the problem is upstream of the analysts — what stage turns raw detections into workable signal?
objectives: Apply tuning/enrichment to reduce alert fatigue
evidence: Redesigned the alert pipeline with tuning, dedup, enrichment, and risk scoring before ticketing

scenarios.title: Incident Response as a Feedback System
scenarios.situation: A company has handled three separate phishing-to-ransomware incidents in six months. Each time the IR team contained and recovered well, but the same entry vector keeps working. The CISO asks why incidents keep recurring despite good response.
scenarios.prompt: Viewing IR as a system, what is broken?
choices: The containment phase — they should isolate faster
The lessons-learned phase isn't feeding back into prevention: findings aren't becoming new controls, training, or detection rules
The eradication phase — malware keeps surviving
They need a bigger IR team
scenarios.why: Incident response is a closed-loop system: preparation → detection → containment → eradication → recovery → lessons learned → back into preparation. When the loop is open — lessons learned produces a report that nobody converts into hardened email filtering, phishing simulations, MFA enforcement, or new SIEM rules — each incident is handled well but the system never learns, so the same attack re-enters. Faster containment or more staff improves the response without changing the recurrence; the missing feedback arrow is the defect.
scenarios.hint: Good response, same incident three times — which IR phase is supposed to make the NEXT attack harder?
objectives: Model IR as a feedback loop
evidence: Identified the broken lessons-learned feedback loop behind recurring incidents
