scenarios.title: PBQ: The Log That Tells the Story
scenarios.situation: You are given 20 lines of Windows Security event logs. User 'jsmith' has 47 failed logons (4625) in 10 minutes from a single external IP, then one success (4624), then three new scheduled tasks created. The exam asks: what happened, and what is the FIRST response action?
scenarios.prompt: What occurred, and what is the FIRST thing you should do?
choices: Brute-force succeeded; immediately reset jsmith's password and revoke sessions
Password spraying across users; block the source IP at the firewall and move on
Brute-force succeeded; first preserve evidence (memory/log export), then contain the host
Normal admin activity; failed logons are expected noise, no action needed
scenarios.why: 47 failures then a success from one external IP is textbook brute force that worked — and the scheduled tasks signal persistence. But the FIRST action is evidence preservation: memory and logs are volatile, and containment that wipes the host destroys the forensics. Preserve, then contain, then eradicate. The exam tests this order relentlessly.
scenarios.hint: What does the sequence failures→success→persistence tell you? And what is fragile enough to lose if you act rashly?
evidence: Security log excerpt
4625 x47 (jsmith, 10 min, single IP) → 4624 success → 4698 scheduled task created x3
EDR status
Host online, no isolation yet. Memory capture not yet taken.

scenarios.title: The 90-Minute Budget
scenarios.situation: You sit down for Security+: up to 90 questions in 90 minutes, including several performance-based questions (PBQs) that each can take 5-10 minutes. Twenty minutes in, you've answered 12 questions and are stuck on a tricky log-analysis PBQ.
scenarios.prompt: What is the best time-management move right now?
choices: Finish the PBQ no matter what — it's worth more points
Flag the PBQ, move on, and answer all multiple-choice first; return to PBQs with remaining time
Rush through the next 20 questions to catch up
Skip every PBQ entirely and focus on multiple choice
scenarios.why: PBQs are time-expensive but not worth sacrificing dozens of multiple-choice questions you can answer quickly — each unanswered question is a guaranteed zero. The winning strategy is two passes: sweep the multiple-choice (roughly a minute each) to bank points, then spend remaining time on PBQs where partial credit is possible. Rushing creates careless errors on easy points, and skipping PBQs abandons partial-credit opportunities. Flag-and-return keeps both point sources alive.
scenarios.hint: Every blank answer scores zero — which approach banks the most certain points first?
evidence: Applied a two-pass time strategy that prioritizes bankable multiple-choice points

scenarios.title: Attacking a Firewall-Rule PBQ
scenarios.situation: A PBQ shows a network diagram and asks you to drag firewall rules into the correct order to allow web traffic to a DMZ server while blocking everything else. There are six rule tiles and the interface is unfamiliar.
scenarios.prompt: What is the best approach to this PBQ?
choices: Place the rules in the order that 'looks right' and submit quickly to save time
Read the goal first, identify the required allows, put the specific allows before the final deny-all, then verify each traffic flow against your ordering
Put deny-all first to be safe, then the allow rules
Skip it — PBQs are experimental and don't count
scenarios.why: PBQs reward method: state the goal, translate it into rule logic (firewalls evaluate top-down, first match wins), place specific allows before the terminal deny-all, then mentally test each required flow — 'does HTTPS from internet reach the DMZ? does anything else get through?' Deny-first blocks everything below it; 'looks right' wastes the partial credit these questions offer; and PBQs absolutely count. The verification pass is what converts a guess into points.
scenarios.hint: Firewalls read rules top-down, first match wins — how must allows and the final deny be ordered?
evidence: Constructed and verified a top-down firewall rule ordering in a PBQ

scenarios.title: Elimination Under Pressure
scenarios.situation: Question 47: 'Which control BEST mitigates credential theft via phishing?' The options are: A) Annual security awareness training, B) Mandatory MFA on all remote access, C) A stronger password complexity policy, D) Quarterly phishing simulations. You're unsure between two of them with 40 seconds left.
scenarios.prompt: What is the best elimination reasoning?
choices: Pick the longest answer — longest is usually correct
Eliminate C (passwords don't stop phishing credential reuse well) and A/D (awareness helps but is weaker than a technical control), leaving B — MFA neutralizes stolen credentials
Pick A because training is the cheapest control
Choose randomly — all four sound plausible
scenarios.why: Elimination works by comparing control strength against the threat mechanism: phishing steals credentials, and MFA makes stolen credentials insufficient — a technical control that directly breaks the attack chain. Complexity policies don't stop harvested passwords from being reused; awareness training and simulations reduce click rates but never to zero, making them weaker 'best' answers. The exam constantly asks for the BEST/MOST effective control, which usually means the technical control that neutralizes the mechanism, not the cheapest or most educational one.
scenarios.hint: The question asks what BEST mitigates stolen credentials — which option makes a stolen password useless?
evidence: Eliminated weaker controls to select the mechanism-neutralizing answer

scenarios.title: Flag, Don't Sink
scenarios.situation: Question 23 describes a complex multi-site VPN and PKI scenario with a long paragraph. You've read it twice and still can't pin down what's being asked. The clock shows you've spent 3 minutes on it.
scenarios.prompt: What should you do?
choices: Read it a third time carefully — understanding will come
Flag it, pick your best guess for now, move on, and return with fresh eyes if time remains
Leave it blank and come back — a blank is better than a wrong guess
Ask the proctor for clarification on the scenario
scenarios.why: Three minutes on one question is a budget emergency: at that burn rate you forfeit multiple easier questions. Flag-and-guess preserves the possibility of points (there's no penalty for wrong answers) while freeing you to bank certain points elsewhere; returning later often unlocks the question because subsequent questions prime relevant concepts. Leaving it blank guarantees zero, re-reading under stress rarely helps, and proctors can't explain content.
scenarios.hint: No penalty for wrong answers, and every minute has an opportunity cost — what preserves both?
evidence: Flagged a time-sink question with a provisional answer instead of burning the time budget

scenarios.title: Parsing the Scenario Question
scenarios.situation: A question gives you a half-page scenario: company size, industry, three systems, two recent incidents, a budget constraint, and a compliance requirement. The final sentence asks: 'Which of the following should the analyst do FIRST?'
scenarios.prompt: What is the most reliable parsing technique?
choices: Memorize every detail in the paragraph before looking at the options
Read the final question sentence first, identify the action word (FIRST/NEXT/BEST), then scan the scenario only for facts relevant to sequencing
Pick the answer mentioning the compliance requirement — compliance always wins
Choose the most technically advanced option
scenarios.why: Scenario questions bury the actual task in context — the final sentence defines it. Reading it first tells you what to hunt for: 'FIRST' means sequencing/triage logic (contain before eradicate, identify before contain), so you scan for facts that order actions and ignore decorative detail. Compliance and advanced tech are classic distractors that feel important but don't answer 'what comes first in the workflow.' Question-first parsing cuts through the noise reliably.
scenarios.hint: The last sentence is the real question — what does the word FIRST tell you to look for?
evidence: Used question-first parsing to isolate the sequencing task in a scenario question

scenarios.title: Spotting the Distractor Pattern
scenarios.situation: Four answer choices for an incident-response question: A) 'Immediately wipe and rebuild all 500 workstations,' B) 'Isolate affected hosts and preserve volatile memory for analysis,' C) 'Ignore the alert; it's probably a false positive,' D) 'Shut down the entire corporate network.'
scenarios.prompt: Which pattern identifies the distractors here?
choices: The correct answer is always the middle option
Extreme, absolute, or disproportionate actions (wipe everything, shut down everything, ignore entirely) are classic distractors; the measured, procedural option is usually correct
The longest option is always the distractor
Options with technical terms are distractors
scenarios.why: CompTIA distractors follow patterns: absolutes ('always,' 'never,' 'all,' 'immediately wipe everything') and disproportionate responses signal wrong answers, because real security practice is measured and procedural. Option B follows the actual IR sequence — contain, preserve evidence — while A and D nuke availability for no reason and C abandons duty of care. Recognizing the 'extreme action' pattern lets you eliminate two or three options in seconds, even when you're unsure of the exact right answer.
scenarios.hint: Which options nuke everything or do nothing — and what does real incident response actually look like?
evidence: Eliminated extreme-action distractors to identify the procedural IR answer

scenarios.title: Test-Day Final Decisions
scenarios.situation: You've finished all 90 questions with 12 minutes left. You flagged 8 questions. On review, one flagged answer 'feels' wrong but you can't articulate why, and another you now think you misread.
scenarios.prompt: What is the evidence-based review strategy?
choices: Change every flagged answer — first instincts are usually wrong
Never change any answer — first instincts are usually right
Change only answers where re-reading reveals a concrete misread or new understanding; leave 'feels wrong' gut changes alone
Submit immediately — reviewing only causes second-guessing
scenarios.why: Research on answer-changing shows changes help when driven by new information (you misread 'FIRST' as 'BEST,' you recall the port number correctly on second thought) and hurt when driven by anxiety alone. The disciplined rule: re-read each flagged question fully, change only if you can state the specific reason, and use remaining time to verify you answered every question rather than churning guesses. Abandoning review wastes the easiest points on the exam — catching misreads.
scenarios.hint: Gut feelings mislead; concrete re-reads don't — what distinguishes a good change from a bad one?
evidence: Changed only answers with a concrete, articulable reason during review

domains.name: SOC Analyst Playbook
domains.description: Think like a Tier 1 SOC analyst: triage alerts, escalate with context, and run the first 15 minutes of any incident.

scenarios.title: The Alert That Needed Context
scenarios.situation: 02:14: IDS flags 'possible data exfiltration' — 4GB outbound to an unknown IP from the backup server. The Tier 1 analyst is about to page the CISO. You are the shift lead.
scenarios.prompt: Apply the three triage questions. What is your call?
choices: Page the CISO immediately — 4GB to an unknown IP is always critical
Correlate first: check whether the destination is the contracted cloud backup endpoint and whether a backup window is scheduled — then decide
Block the IP at the firewall and isolate the backup server now
Close as false positive — backup servers always send large outbound transfers
scenarios.why: Is it real? A backup server sending 4GB at 02:14 smells like a scheduled cloud backup, not exfiltration — but 'smells like' is not an answer. Correlate: destination IP vs contracted endpoint, backup schedule, job logs. If it matches, it is expected behavior (tune the rule). If not, THEN escalate with the correlation attached. The discipline is: second source before siren.
scenarios.hint: What is the backup server SUPPOSED to do at 2 AM? Check that before anything else.
evidence: IDS alert
4GB outbound, backup-srv-01 → 203.0.113.44 (unknown), 02:14
Backup schedule
Cloud backup window: 02:00–04:00 nightly to contracted endpoint.

scenarios.title: Triage: Which Alert Burns First
scenarios.situation: Monday 8 AM, the queue holds: (1) critical-severity malware alert on a receptionist's PC, (2) medium-severity 'impossible travel' login for the CFO's account, (3) high-severity port scan against a DMZ web server, (4) critical-severity alert for Mimikatz-like behavior on a domain controller.
scenarios.prompt: In what order should the analyst triage these?
choices: 1, 3, 4, 2 — work criticals first in arrival order
4, 2, 1, 3 — domain controller compromise and executive account takeover outrank workstation malware and noisy scans
3, 1, 2, 4 — external-facing issues first
2, 4, 3, 1 — user accounts before systems
scenarios.why: Triage ranks by blast radius and asset criticality, not raw severity or arrival order. A domain controller showing credential-dumping behavior threatens the entire identity infrastructure — that's an enterprise-wide compromise in progress. The CFO's impossible-travel login suggests executive account takeover with access to sensitive data. Workstation malware is contained to one host; port scans against a DMZ are constant background noise. Severity labels without asset and impact context mislead; triage must weigh what falls if the alert is real.
scenarios.hint: Forget the severity labels for a moment — if each alert is real, which one costs the company the most?
objectives: Prioritize alerts by impact and asset criticality
evidence: Triaged a mixed alert queue by blast radius, ranking DC compromise first

scenarios.title: Escalation: L1 to Incident Response
scenarios.situation: An L1 analyst sees an alert: PowerShell downloading an encoded payload on an HR workstation, followed by outbound connections to an unknown external IP. The user says they 'just opened a resume.' The playbook says L1 can handle isolated adware, but must escalate suspected command-and-control.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct escalation decision?
choices: Close it as user-initiated adware — the user admitted opening the file
Escalate to L2/IR immediately: encoded PowerShell plus outbound C2-like connections meets the escalation criterion regardless of the user's story
Quarantine the host and wait to see if more alerts fire before escalating
Email the user asking them not to open resumes anymore
scenarios.why: Escalation criteria exist so L1 doesn't have to be certain — the pattern (encoded PowerShell download + external beaconing) matches the playbook's C2 definition, and user explanations never override technical indicators (attackers rely on exactly this social cover). Waiting for more alerts gives the adversary dwell time to move laterally. The analyst's job is to recognize the pattern matches the escalation threshold and hand off with full context, not to investigate to certainty alone.
scenarios.hint: The playbook defines what gets escalated — does this pattern match it, no matter what the user says?
objectives: Distinguish L1 containment from IR handoff
evidence: Escalated a C2-pattern alert to IR per playbook criteria despite user explanation

scenarios.title: SIEM Query: Hunting Lateral Movement
scenarios.situation: Threat intel reports a group that, after initial access, moves laterally using SMB and WMI with stolen credentials, typically within 2 hours of landing. The SOC lead asks you to write a hunt query covering the last 7 days.
scenarios.prompt: What query logic best hunts this behavior?
choices: Search all firewall logs for any blocked outbound traffic in the last 7 days
Correlate: successful logons (event 4624, type 3/10) to a host, followed within 2 hours by that same account making SMB (445) or WMI (135) connections to additional hosts it never touched before
Alert on every PowerShell execution across the fleet
Search email gateways for phishing lures from the last 7 days
scenarios.why: Threat hunting translates adversary behavior into log correlation: the intel gives you the technique (SMB/WMI lateral movement), the timing (within 2 hours), and the anomaly (new host-to-host paths). A good hunt query joins authentication logs with network connection logs on account + time window + first-seen host pairs — that finds the behavior whether or not any signature fired. Firewall blocks and blanket PowerShell alerts are too noisy or miss the point; email lures hunt the wrong phase (initial access, not lateral movement).
scenarios.hint: The intel describes a sequence: logon, then new connections, within a time window — what logs, joined how, would reveal that sequence?
evidence: Wrote a correlated hunt query for SMB/WMI lateral movement within a 2-hour window

scenarios.title: Ticket Prioritization Matrix
scenarios.situation: Two tickets land simultaneously. Ticket A: ransomware detected on a single kiosk PC in the lobby (low business value, isolated VLAN). Ticket B: suspicious OAuth consent grants on the CEO's mailbox (no malware, but potential email takeover). The SLA matrix scores impact x urgency.
scenarios.prompt: How should they be prioritized?
choices: Ticket A first — ransomware is always the top priority word
Ticket B first — a mailbox takeover of the CEO has far higher impact (fraud, data theft, reputation) even without malware
Work both simultaneously — priority matrices don't apply to security
Ticket A first — it has the scarier alert name
scenarios.why: The impact x urgency matrix exists precisely to defeat scary-word bias. Ticket A's blast radius is one isolated, low-value kiosk — high urgency word, low actual impact. Ticket B threatens the CEO's entire communications, enabling wire fraud, sensitive data access, and reputational damage — high impact even at moderate urgency. Prioritization must score the business consequence of the alert being real, not react to the alert's vocabulary.
scenarios.hint: Score each ticket: if real, what does the business actually lose?
evidence: Prioritized a CEO mailbox-takeover ticket over isolated kiosk ransomware via impact scoring

scenarios.title: The Shift Handoff Note
scenarios.situation: Your 12-hour SOC shift ends. During it you: triaged 60 alerts, escalated one possible C2 case (host isolated, IR engaged, awaiting forensics), tuned a noisy rule, and noticed a slow uptick in failed VPN logins from one country that hasn't crossed any threshold yet.
scenarios.prompt: What belongs in the handoff note to the next shift?
choices: A full list of all 60 alerts triaged, in order
The escalated C2 case status and next expected action, the rule tuned (so they know alert volume changed), and the VPN-login uptick as a watch item with the current count
Just the C2 escalation — everything else is routine
Nothing — the ticketing system has it all
scenarios.why: A handoff transfers state the next analyst can't reconstruct: open investigations and their pending next steps, environmental changes (a tuned rule changes what the queue looks like — without this note the next shift misreads volume changes), and sub-threshold trends that only become visible across shifts. A 60-alert dump is noise; 'nothing' assumes the next analyst will discover the trend from scratch; C2-only omits the context that prevents tomorrow's miss. Good handoffs carry open loops, changed baselines, and emerging patterns.
scenarios.hint: What would the next analyst need to know that they can't figure out from the ticket queue alone?
evidence: Wrote a handoff covering open escalation, baseline change, and a sub-threshold trend

scenarios.title: Tuning the Noisy Rule
scenarios.situation: A SIEM rule 'Mass file encryption detected' fires 300 times a day — 299 are the backup agent compressing archives at 2 AM, and 1 last month was real ransomware caught late because analysts had muted the rule's notifications out of fatigue.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct tuning action?
choices: Delete the rule — it's 99.7% false positives
Keep the rule as-is and tell analysts to pay more attention
Tune the rule: exclude the known backup agent process/path, add a velocity or entropy threshold, and keep alerting on the remainder
Lower the rule's severity so it stops paging anyone
scenarios.why: False-positive tuning is surgery, not amputation: the rule detects a genuinely critical behavior, so deleting it blinds you to ransomware, and muting it (what analysts did informally) caused the late catch. The fix adds context the rule lacks — allowlist the known-good backup process, require stronger signals (encryption velocity, entropy, mass extension renames) — so the 299 benign firings stop and the 1 real one pages loudly. Severity-lowering without tuning just changes which queue the noise lands in.
scenarios.hint: The rule's logic is right but too broad — how do you keep the detection while removing the known-benign pattern?
evidence: Tuned a noisy ransomware rule with allowlisting and thresholds instead of disabling it

scenarios.title: Threat Hunting Hypothesis
scenarios.situation: Your threat intel feed reports a ransomware affiliate targeting healthcare, entering via exposed RDP, then disabling backup services before encrypting. Your hospital has RDP exposed on two jump hosts 'temporarily' for a vendor, and backups run nightly.
scenarios.prompt: What is the best-structured hunt hypothesis?
choices: Search for ransomware — it's the biggest threat

Hypothesis: the affiliate is already inside via the exposed RDP jump hosts; hunt for RDP logons from unusual sources followed by backup-service tampering (event logs for stopped VSS/backup services) on servers
Block RDP at the firewall and consider the hunt done
Scan the whole network for malware signatures
scenarios.why: Hypothesis-driven hunting starts from intel + your own exposure and predicts the adversary's observable steps: IF they're inside via our known-exposed RDP, THEN we'd see anomalous RDP logons followed by backup tampering (their pre-encryption ritual). That gives you specific logs to query (RDP 4624s, service-stop events) and a falsifiable outcome. 'Search for ransomware' is unfocused; blocking RDP is remediation, not hunting (and doesn't tell you if they're already in); signature scanning hunts tools, not the described behavior chain.
scenarios.hint: A good hypothesis names the entry point you actually have exposed and the observable steps the intel says come next.
objectives: Map intel TTPs to log evidence
evidence: Built a falsifiable hunt hypothesis linking exposed RDP to backup-tampering indicators

domains.name: Cryptography in Practice
domains.description: Beyond definitions: key management lifecycles, certificate troubleshooting, and crypto agility decisions.

scenarios.title: The Expired Certificate at the Worst Moment
scenarios.situation: Monday 08:00: the VPN portal shows a certificate error for all users. The certificate expired Sunday at midnight. Auto-renewal was 'configured'. The help desk is drowning.
scenarios.prompt: What failed in the key lifecycle, and what are the immediate and permanent fixes?
choices: Generation failed — the CA is down; rebuild the PKI immediately
Rotation failed — auto-renewal silently broke; emergency-renew now, then add expiry alerting and test renewals
Revocation failed — the old cert was not revoked; revoke it and the error clears
Distribution failed — push the new cert to clients via GPO
scenarios.why: The certificate lived its full life and died on schedule — the failure is rotation: renewal was assumed but never verified. Immediate: emergency renewal and deployment. Permanent: expiry alerting at 30/14/7 days plus a tested, monitored auto-renewal. Every lifecycle stage needs an owner and a monitor; 'configured' without verification is hope, not a control.
scenarios.hint: The cert did exactly what certs do. Which lifecycle stage was supposed to prevent this moment?
evidence: Cert details
vpn.corp.local — valid to Sunday 00:00, now expired. Issuer: internal CA.
Renewal logs
Auto-renewal task last succeeded 400 days ago; last 3 runs errored silently.

scenarios.title: Killing Old TLS
scenarios.situation: A vulnerability scan flags the company's public web servers for supporting TLS 1.0 and 1.1. The e-commerce team worries that disabling them will break old customer browsers, but the compliance team says auditors will fail them if the protocols stay enabled.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct decision?
choices: Keep TLS 1.0/1.1 enabled — customer compatibility comes first
Disable TLS 1.0 and 1.1, keep TLS 1.2 and 1.3; publish a deprecation notice and monitor handshake failures for genuinely affected clients
Disable all TLS and switch the site to plain HTTP for maximum compatibility
Enable SSL 3.0 as a fallback for the oldest clients
scenarios.why: TLS 1.0 and 1.1 are deprecated (RFC 8996) with known vulnerabilities like BEAST, and PCI DSS requires 1.2+ — keeping them fails audits and exposes customers. TLS 1.2 (properly configured) and 1.3 cover effectively all modern clients; the compatibility risk is real but measurable, so you deprecate with notice and monitor rather than guessing. Plain HTTP or SSL 3.0 (POODLE) would be catastrophic downgrades. Crypto decisions weigh protocol security against measured — not feared — compatibility impact.
scenarios.hint: Two of these protocol versions are formally deprecated and audit-failing — which ones, and what's the safe floor?
evidence: Chose to disable TLS 1.0/1.1 while retaining 1.2/1.3 with monitored deprecation

scenarios.title: The Certificate Name Mismatch
scenarios.situation: After a website migration, users get browser warnings: 'certificate name mismatch.' The certificate is valid, unexpired, issued by a trusted public CA — but it was issued for shop.example.com while the site now also serves customers at store.example.com.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct fix?
choices: Tell users to click through the warning — the certificate is valid
Reissue the certificate with a Subject Alternative Name (SAN) covering both shop.example.com and store.example.com
Disable HTTPS on store.example.com to stop the warnings
Install the same certificate on more servers
scenarios.why: TLS clients validate that the certificate's subject matches the hostname in the URL bar — the modern mechanism is the Subject Alternative Name extension, which can list multiple DNS names on one certificate. A name mismatch means the presented identity doesn't match the requested site, and training users to click through destroys the entire authentication value of TLS (attackers rely on exactly that habit). Reissuing with proper SANs is the fix; disabling HTTPS or duplicating the wrong cert doesn't address the identity mismatch.
scenarios.hint: The certificate proves identity — but for which name? What certificate field lists all the names it covers?
evidence: Diagnosed a name-mismatch warning and prescribed SAN reissuance

scenarios.title: Keys After the Admin Leaves
scenarios.situation: The sole systems administrator — who personally generated and held the company's disk-encryption recovery keys, the CA's offline root key passphrase, and several service-account API keys — resigns abruptly on bad terms. Nothing appears compromised, but he had full access until his last day.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct key-management response?
choices: Do nothing — there's no evidence of compromise

Rotate all keys and credentials he could have accessed or copied: reissue API keys, rotate service passwords, re-key encryption where feasible, and change CA operational credentials under dual control
Just disable his user account
Change only the keys he explicitly asks about in the exit interview
scenarios.why: Key management treats privileged departure as a compromise of key confidentiality by default: keys he held must be considered known to him, and 'no evidence of misuse' is not evidence of safety. Rotation must be comprehensive (everything he touched, not just what he mentions) and the new key custody must enforce separation of duties — no more single-person key holdings, with the root CA key under dual control in an HSM or safe. Disabling the account stops future logins but does nothing about keys already in his possession.
scenarios.hint: He doesn't need his account to use a copied key — what does that imply about which keys are still trustworthy?
objectives: Apply key rotation on personnel change
Enforce separation of duties in key custody
evidence: Ordered comprehensive key rotation and dual-control custody after privileged departure

scenarios.title: Hashing: Passwords vs File Integrity
scenarios.situation: A developer proposes using SHA-256 for everything: storing user passwords as SHA-256 hashes and verifying software downloads with SHA-256 checksums. A reviewer flags half of this plan.
scenarios.prompt: Which half is wrong, and what should replace it?
choices: Both uses are fine — SHA-256 is secure for everything
Password storage is the problem: fast hashes like SHA-256 fall to GPU brute force, so passwords need a slow, salted KDF like bcrypt/argon2; SHA-256 checksums for file integrity are correct
File integrity is the problem: checksums should use MD5 for speed; password hashing with SHA-256 is fine
Replace both with encryption — hashing is obsolete
scenarios.why: Hashing choices depend on the threat model. Password storage faces offline brute-force attacks where the attacker has the hash — fast hashes (SHA-256 does billions/sec on GPUs) collapse, so you need deliberately slow, salted, memory-hard functions (bcrypt, argon2, PBKDF2) that make each guess expensive. File-integrity verification faces a different threat (detecting tampering), where SHA-256's collision resistance and speed are exactly right. MD5 is broken for integrity (collisions); encryption doesn't replace hashing (different purpose — reversibility vs one-way verification).
scenarios.hint: One use case gives the attacker unlimited fast guesses; the other just needs tamper evidence — which needs slowness?
objectives: Choose hashing algorithms by use case
evidence: Selected bcrypt/argon2 for passwords and SHA-256 for integrity based on threat models

scenarios.title: Designing the Internal PKI
scenarios.situation: A 500-person company wants an internal PKI for VPN client certs, Wi-Fi (EAP-TLS), and code signing. The proposed design: a single online root CA on a domain-joined server, issuing directly to end users, with the CA admin also approving their own certificate requests.
scenarios.prompt: What are the critical design fixes?
choices: The design is fine — one CA keeps it simple
Take the root CA offline (air-gapped, powered down except for rare signing), use online intermediate CAs for day-to-day issuance, and enforce separation of duties on approvals
Buy public certificates for everything instead
Make the root CA highly available with 99.99% uptime
scenarios.why: PKI security concentrates in the root: whoever controls the root key can mint trusted identities for the entire organization, so the root must be offline (minimizing exposure) with intermediates handling daily issuance (so a compromised intermediate can be revoked without rebuilding trust). Separation of duties prevents a single admin from self-approving fraudulent certs. A public CA can't issue for internal-only names/purposes cost-effectively and outsources your internal trust; high-availability on the root increases its attack surface — the opposite of what's wanted.
scenarios.hint: The root key is the crown jewel — should it be online issuing certs daily, or locked away with subordinates doing the work?
objectives: Apply root protection and separation of duties
evidence: Redesigned PKI with offline root, intermediates, and separation of duties

scenarios.title: Encryption at Rest vs in Transit
scenarios.situation: A startup stores customer PII in a cloud database, replicates it to analysts' laptops for reporting, and serves it through a web API. The founder says 'we use HTTPS, so the data is encrypted' and considers the job done.
scenarios.prompt: What is the encryption gap analysis?
choices: HTTPS is sufficient — encryption is encryption
HTTPS covers in-transit only; they also need at-rest encryption (database/volume encryption) and protection for the laptop copies (full-disk encryption, or better: stop replicating PII to laptops)
They need to encrypt the HTTPS traffic a second time
At-rest encryption is unnecessary in the cloud — the provider handles everything
scenarios.why: Encryption has three states and each needs its own control: in-transit (TLS/HTTPS — they have this), at-rest (volume/database encryption for the cloud DB — protects against stolen disks, snapshots, misconfigured storage), and the endpoint copies on laptops, which are the highest-risk state (lost/stolen devices). The founder's mental model covers one of three. The strongest fix for the laptops isn't just FDE — it's eliminating the PII replication entirely (analysts query masked views), removing the risk rather than encrypting it.
scenarios.hint: HTTPS protects data moving across the wire — what protects it sitting on the disk, or on a laptop left in a taxi?
objectives: Apply data minimization to endpoint risk
evidence: Identified missing at-rest and endpoint encryption beyond existing TLS coverage

scenarios.title: Crypto Agility: The Algorithm Sunset
scenarios.situation: The company's flagship product hardcodes SHA-1 for document signatures and RSA-1024 for license keys deep in the codebase and in shipped client software. Industry bodies have deprecated both, and a major customer now contractually requires SHA-256 minimum and quantum-readiness planning.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct crypto-agility response?
choices: Do nothing until an actual break is demonstrated — deprecation is theoretical
Patch just the server side to SHA-256 and leave shipped clients as-is

Plan a migration: abstract crypto into a swappable module, ship dual-support (accept old, prefer new) during transition, reissue signatures/keys, and roadmap post-quantum algorithms — treating algorithm agility as an architecture property
Switch everything to a proprietary in-house cipher to avoid standards churn
scenarios.why: Crypto agility is the architectural ability to replace algorithms without rebuilding the product — hardcoded primitives are the anti-pattern that turns every deprecation into a crisis. The migration needs a transition strategy (dual support avoids bricking shipped clients overnight), re-issuance of artifacts signed with weak algorithms, and forward planning for post-quantum migration. Server-only patching leaves the trust chain broken at the client; in-house ciphers violate Kerckhoffs's principle and every audit standard; waiting for a demonstrated break means migrating during an active compromise.
scenarios.hint: Hardcoded algorithms turn every deprecation into a rewrite — what architecture property would have made this a config change?
evidence: Designed an algorithm migration with abstraction, dual support, and PQC roadmap

domains.name: Incident Response Tabletop
domains.description: Walk full incident lifecycles: preparation through lessons-learned, with tabletop scenarios from real breach patterns.

scenarios.title: Ransomware: Scope Before Sirens
scenarios.situation: 09:12: help desk reports 'weird file extensions' on two accounting workstations. By 09:20 there are four. Someone suggests shutting down the file server 'just in case'.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct sequence for the next 30 minutes?
choices: Shut down the file server and all workstations immediately to stop the spread
Scope first: identify patient zero and lateral movement via EDR/logs, isolate affected hosts from network (not power off), verify backup isolation, then declare
Start restoring from backup right away — speed matters most
Wipe the four workstations and reimage; the file server is probably fine
scenarios.why: Scope before sirens: you cannot contain what you have not mapped. Isolate affected hosts at the network layer (power-off kills memory forensics), verify the backups are isolated and clean BEFORE touching them, identify patient zero for the eradication plan. Shutting down the file server blindly may destroy evidence and does nothing if the spread vector is elsewhere. Restore comes after eradication — restoring into a still-infected environment just re-encrypts.
scenarios.hint: What do you lose if you power off? What do you risk if you restore too early?
evidence: EDR console
4 hosts with mass-rename behavior; file server clean so far; C2 beacon from WS-011.
Backup status
Backup server reachable; last night's backup completed; isolation not yet verified.

scenarios.title: The CEO's Urgent Email
scenarios.situation: Finance wired $38,000 to a 'new vendor' after an urgent email from the CEO. The CEO says they never sent it. The finance mailbox has a new forwarding rule to an external address.
scenarios.prompt: What is the full containment sequence?
choices: Reset the finance user's password and delete the forwarding rule
Disable account + revoke all sessions/tokens + remove malicious rules + place litigation hold + hunt all mailboxes for the same IOCs
Block the external forwarding domain at the mail gateway
Call the bank to reverse the wire and close the ticket
scenarios.why: BEC persistence survives password resets: active sessions, OAuth tokens, and mailbox rules all persist. Full containment is account disable, session/token revocation, rule removal, and litigation hold for forensics — then hunt every mailbox for the same forwarding-rule IOC before declaring victory. The bank call happens in parallel, but it is recovery, not containment. Miss the hunt step and the attacker still has a foothold.
scenarios.hint: What survives a password reset? List every persistence mechanism before choosing.
evidence: Mailbox rules
Finance mailbox: rule 'AutoFwd' forwards all mail to attacker@external.example; created 06:12.
Sign-in logs
Impossible travel: logon from home city 08:00, foreign IP 08:07. No MFA challenge recorded.

scenarios.title: Scoping the Compromised Account
scenarios.situation: The help desk confirms a sales rep's credentials were phished. The attacker logged into webmail and the VPN over 6 hours. The rep had access to the CRM, the file share, and (via a shared admin password the team passed around) two servers.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct scoping approach?
choices: Reset the rep's password and close the ticket — the account is the scope

Scope to everything the credentials could touch: review VPN/webmail/CRM/file-share logs for the attacker's session, treat the shared admin password as compromised (rotate it, check both servers), and expand if logs show lateral movement
Wipe the rep's laptop immediately
Notify all customers that their data was stolen
scenarios.why: Scoping answers 'how far did it go' by following the credentials' reach, not the user's story: every system those credentials (and the shared admin password) can access is in scope until logs prove otherwise. The shared password is critical — its compromise extends scope to both servers and anyone else who used it. Wiping the laptop destroys evidence before scoping; customer notification before knowing what was accessed is premature and potentially legally mishandled. Scope via log review of each reachable system, then contain.
scenarios.hint: The scope isn't the person — it's every system those credentials (including the shared one) could reach.
objectives: Scope an incident via credential reach
evidence: Scoped a phishing incident across all systems reachable by compromised and shared credentials

scenarios.title: Contain: Pull the Plug or Isolate?
scenarios.situation: A database server shows active ransomware encryption in progress — files renaming by the second. The server holds the only copy of today's transactions (backup runs at midnight). The network team can either yank the power/network cable now or do a graceful host isolation via EDR.
scenarios.prompt: What is the best containment choice?
choices: Pull the power immediately — stop the encryption at all costs
Isolate the host from the network via EDR/switch port shutdown while keeping it powered on, preserving volatile memory for forensics
Let it finish encrypting so you have a 'complete' incident to analyze
Disconnect the backups first, then decide
scenarios.why: Containment must stop the bleeding without destroying evidence or recovery options. Network isolation (EDR quarantine, port shutdown) halts spread and C2 while preserving RAM — which holds encryption keys, process lists, and network connections that forensics and possible decryption need. Yanking power kills volatile evidence and risks database corruption on top of the encryption; letting it finish is negligence; and the backups should already be isolated/offline by design — touching them mid-incident risks the recovery path.
scenarios.hint: You need to stop the spread AND keep what's in memory — which action does both?
evidence: Selected network isolation over power-pull to preserve volatile forensic evidence

scenarios.title: Preserving the Evidence
scenarios.situation: HR reports a departing employee may have exfiltrated customer lists to a personal USB drive. The employee's workstation is still powered on at their desk. Legal wants the evidence to hold up if this goes to court.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct evidence-preservation sequence?
choices: Let HR search the desk and copy interesting files to a thumb drive for legal

Photograph the scene, capture volatile data (RAM, network connections) first per order of volatility, then create a forensic bit-stream image with a write blocker, hash it, and maintain chain of custody
Turn the workstation off immediately to 'freeze' everything
Remote-wipe the machine to prevent further exfiltration
scenarios.why: Forensic soundness follows the order of volatility (RAM and live state first — they vanish at power-off) then a bit-for-bit image through a write blocker so the original is never altered, with cryptographic hashes proving the copy matches and a chain-of-custody log proving who handled it. HR copying files alters timestamps and destroys admissibility; powering off kills the volatile evidence (open connections, mounted drives, in-memory artifacts); wiping is destruction of evidence and potentially a crime. Legal admissibility requires provable non-alteration at every step.
scenarios.hint: Courts ask 'prove you didn't change anything' — which sequence creates that proof?
evidence: Sequenced volatile capture, write-blocked imaging, hashing, and chain of custody

scenarios.title: Who Gets Told, and When
scenarios.situation: Forensics confirms attackers accessed a database with 50,000 customer records including SSNs. It's 9 PM. The CEO wants to 'wait until we know everything' before telling anyone. Legal, PR, and the incident commander disagree on timing.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct communication approach?
choices: Wait until the investigation is 100% complete — premature disclosure causes panic

Follow the communication plan: notify legal and executive leadership immediately, prepare customer/regulator notifications on the legally required timelines (state breach laws often 30-60 days), and keep all external messaging through designated spokespeople
Have the SOC analyst tweet about it to get ahead of the story
Tell customers individually as each record is confirmed
scenarios.why: Breach communication is governed by law and plan, not by comfort: most US states require consumer notification within 30-60 days of discovery, and regulators/contractual obligations add their own clocks — 'wait until we know everything' risks legal liability. The IR communication plan designates who speaks (never ad-hoc tweets from analysts), sequences internal (legal, execs) before external, and prepares holding statements while facts develop. Notification content evolves with the investigation, but the timelines start at discovery, not at certainty.
scenarios.hint: Breach-notification clocks start at discovery, not at full understanding — whose timelines govern here?
evidence: Initiated plan-driven notifications on legal timelines instead of waiting for full certainty

scenarios.title: Eradicate or Rebuild?
scenarios.situation: Forensics finds a kernel-mode rootkit on three production servers. The antivirus 'cleaned' the detected files and the servers appear to be behaving normally. The business pushes to put them back in service tonight to avoid downtime.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct eradication decision?
choices: Return them to service — the AV cleaned the malware and they're behaving normally
Rebuild from known-good images/gold builds: a kernel-mode rootkit compromises the OS's own reporting, so 'clean' and 'normal behavior' are untrustworthy; restore data from verified clean backups
Run a second, different antivirus scan to double-check, then return to service
Reinstall only the visibly affected application
scenarios.why: A kernel-mode rootkit subverts the operating system's own perception — every tool running on that OS, including AV and 'normal behavior' observations, reports through compromised eyes. 'Cleaned' is meaningless when the cleaner can't trust what it sees. The only trustworthy eradication is rebuilding from known-good media and restoring data from backups verified predating the compromise. Business pressure for uptime is real, but returning a rootkitted server to production risks re-infection, persistent access, and a far worse second incident.
scenarios.hint: If the malware controls the kernel, can any tool on that machine tell you the truth about it?
evidence: Ordered rebuild from known-good media for kernel-compromised servers despite uptime pressure

scenarios.title: The Blameless Postmortem
scenarios.situation: The ransomware incident is closed: entry via unpatched VPN, 4-hour dwell, contained by network isolation, recovered from offline backups. The VP wants a lessons-learned meeting and suggests starting with 'who forgot to patch the VPN.'
scenarios.prompt: How should lessons-learned be run to actually improve security?
choices: Focus on individual accountability — name who missed the patch so it doesn't happen again

Run a blameless review: reconstruct the timeline, identify systemic gaps (patch process, VPN exposure, detection delay), assign corrective actions with owners and dates, and feed them into the risk register and control improvements
Skip the meeting — the incident is over and everyone is tired
Write a one-paragraph summary for the file and move on
scenarios.why: Blameless postmortems work because blame shuts down honesty — engineers hide near-misses when the meeting is a tribunal, and the systemic causes (why was the VPN internet-facing and unpatched? why did detection take 4 hours?) never surface. The output must be structural: timeline, contributing system conditions, and tracked corrective actions (patch SLA enforcement, VPN hardening, backup test restores) with owners and deadlines, fed back into governance. A paragraph or a skipped meeting guarantees the identical incident next quarter — which is exactly what the systems-anatomy feedback loop predicts.
scenarios.hint: Blame finds a person; the next attack exploits a system — which does the review need to fix?
objectives: Convert findings into tracked corrective actions
evidence: Ran a blameless postmortem producing tracked systemic corrective actions

lessons.title: General Security Concepts — Core concepts
concepts: CIA triad: confidentiality keeps data from unauthorized eyes, integrity keeps it from unauthorized change, availability keeps it usable when needed. Every control serves at least one leg — name the leg before you buy the control.

Control families vs functions: families (managerial, technical, operational) say who owns the control; functions (preventive, detective, corrective, compensating) say what it does. A firewall is technical and preventive; a log review is operational and detective.

Symmetric crypto (AES) uses one shared key and is fast — ideal for bulk data. Asymmetric crypto (RSA, ECC) uses public/private key pairs and solves key distribution — ideal for exchanging keys and signing. Real systems combine both.
Hashing (SHA-256) is one-way: it fingerprints data for integrity but cannot be reversed to recover the original. Never confuse it with encryption.

PKI binds identities to public keys via certificates issued by Certificate Authorities. The private key never leaves its owner; the certificate is public. Expiry, revocation, and chain trust are the operational realities.
Non-repudiation comes from digital signatures: hash the data, encrypt the hash with the private key. Anyone can verify with the public key; only the signer could have created it.

example.code:
Analyst: "The database is encrypted, so we're secure."
Reality: encryption covered confidentiality — but the app was down six hours (availability) and nobody noticed altered records (integrity).
example.walkthrough: One control rarely covers the whole triad. Map each risk to the leg it threatens, then check you have controls on all three — this is the habit that turns tool-buying into security architecture.

pitfalls: Common trap: calling encryption a complete solution — it addresses confidentiality, not availability or integrity.
Common trap: treating hashing as encryption — hashes cannot be decrypted, and unsalted fast hashes fall to rainbow tables.
Common trap: emailing private keys or embedding them in code — the private key is the identity; expose it and the certificate is worthless.
Common trap: confusing obfuscation (masking) with cryptographic protection.
lessons.try_it: Hash a file yourself in the Terminal tab →

lessons.title: Threats, Vulnerabilities & Mitigations — Core concepts
concepts: Social engineering exploits people, not systems: phishing (broad), spear phishing (targeted), vishing (voice), smishing (SMS), whaling (executives), and BEC (fraudulent payment instructions). The durable defense is a verification process, not just filters.
Injection attacks happen when untrusted input becomes code: SQL injection via concatenated queries, XSS via unescaped output rendered in browsers. Parameterize queries; encode output.

Malware families: viruses need a host and user action, worms self-propagate, trojans masquerade as legitimate software, ransomware encrypts for extortion, rootkits hide, keyloggers capture input. Name the behavior to pick the response.
Vulnerability scanning finds potential weaknesses at scale; penetration testing proves exploitability under scoped rules of engagement. Scans prioritize, tests validate.

Password attacks: brute force tries many passwords against one account, password spraying tries one password against many accounts, credential stuffing replays breached pairs. MFA defeats all three even when the password falls.

example.code: App log: SELECT * FROM users WHERE name='' OR '1'='1' --' AND pass='...'
example.walkthrough: The attacker's text became part of the SQL command because the app glued input into the query string. Parameterized queries send code and data separately, so input is always treated as a value — the structural fix for an entire class of bugs.

pitfalls: Common trap: believing spam filters stop spear phishing — targeted lures are crafted to pass filters; the callback process is the backstop.
Common trap: thinking MFA makes phishing impossible — stolen session cookies and MFA-fatigue prompts bypass it; pair MFA with alerting.
Common trap: treating a clean vulnerability scan as proof of security — scans list possibilities, not exploitability.
Common trap: paying ransomware first — it funds crime, rarely guarantees decryption, and skips the recovery you should have tested.
lessons.try_it: Reason through a recon scan in the Terminal tab →

lessons.title: Security Architecture — Core concepts
concepts: Zero Trust: never trust, always verify. Every access request is authenticated and authorized on identity, device health, and context; implicit trust from network location is removed.
Segmentation (VLANs, firewall zones, microsegmentation) limits lateral movement. A flat network turns one compromise into total compromise; zones turn it into a contained incident.

Shared responsibility: the provider secures the cloud itself (facilities, hypervisor); the customer secures what they put in it. On IaaS that includes the guest OS and patching; the data is always the customer's.
Cloud models trade control for operational burden: IaaS (manage the VMs), PaaS (manage the app, provider manages the platform), SaaS (use the software). Climb the stack when you lack ops capacity.

Resilience is engineered: redundancy, automatic failover, tested backups (3-2-1 with an offline copy), and no single points of failure on critical paths. Bigger boxes still fail; pairs of boxes survive.
Kill cleartext management: Telnet and FTP expose credentials to anyone on the path. SSH, SFTP, and SCP encrypt the session — there is no modern excuse for the old protocols.

example.code:
Flat network: worm enters via print server → reaches finance in 40 minutes.
Segmented: worm hits the printer VLAN's firewall rule → dies at the boundary.
example.walkthrough: Architecture decides the blast radius before any incident occurs. Segmentation does not prevent the first compromise; it decides how far the second step goes.

pitfalls: Common trap: treating the VPN as a trust boundary — one phished credential inside a flat VPN is the whole network.
Common trap: assuming the cloud provider patches your IaaS guests — the hypervisor is theirs; the OS is yours.
Common trap: backups on the same network as production — ransomware encrypts those first; the offline copy is the real backup.
Common trap: confusing high availability with backup — failover keeps you running; backups let you go back in time.
lessons.try_it: Inspect a certificate in the Terminal tab →

lessons.title: Security Operations — Core concepts
concepts: SIEM value is correlation: joining weak signals from many sources into patterns no single log reveals. Tune rules to the business, or analysts drown in noise.

Incident response lifecycle: preparation, detection and analysis, containment, eradication, recovery, lessons learned. Order matters — wiping before containing destroys evidence and lets the threat spread.
Order of volatility: collect the most ephemeral evidence first — RAM before disk, disk before logs. In-memory malware exists only in memory.
Chain of custody: bag, tag, hash, and document every handler. Evidence you cannot prove is unaltered is evidence you cannot use.
Vulnerability management is risk-based: CVSS scores severity, but asset value, exposure, and threat activity determine what you patch this weekend.
Honeypots and deception give high-fidelity detection: a decoy with no legitimate users means every touch is malicious. Isolate them so they cannot become a pivot.

example.code:
09:02 VPN from new country (low) → 09:07 4.2 GB file read (low) → 09:11 3.8 GB outbound email (low)
Correlation rule EXFIL-PATTERN → CRITICAL
example.walkthrough: No single event justified a page; the sequence did. Correlation turns three routine logs into one investigation — this is the analyst skill the operations domain tests.

pitfalls: Common trap: jumping to eradication — reimaging before containment and evidence collection is the classic self-inflicted wound.
Common trap: patching strictly by CVSS — a 7.5 on the internet-facing payment portal outranks a 9.8 on an isolated lab box.
Common trap: treating SIEM alerts as verdicts — the SIEM proposes; the analyst investigates and disposes.
Common trap: powering off a suspect host first — you just destroyed the volatile evidence.
lessons.try_it: Read an auth log in the Terminal tab →

lessons.title: Security Program Management — Core concepts
concepts: Risk responses: mitigate (reduce it), transfer (insurance, contracts), accept (formal sign-off at the right level), avoid (stop the activity). Every risk needs an owner and a documented choice — ignore is not a response.
Quantitative risk: SLE = asset value x exposure factor; ALE = SLE x annualized rate of occurrence. A control should cost less than the ALE it removes.
Policy hierarchy flows down: policies state management intent, standards set mandatory rules, procedures give step-by-step instructions, guidelines recommend. Auditors test the chain.
Third-party risk: assess vendors (questionnaires, SOC 2 reports), bind them contractually (breach notification, audit rights, data return), and grant least-privilege access with monitoring.
Compliance follows the data: GDPR for EU personal data, PCI-DSS for cardholder data, HIPAA for health information. Know your data and your customers' locations.
Awareness is measured by behavior change: baseline click rates, train, re-simulate, track the trend. Punishment drives reporting underground.
BIA sets RTO (how fast back) and RPO (how much data loss tolerable) per system, which drives how much recovery you buy for each tier.

example.code:
Asset $200,000 x EF 25% = SLE $50,000
SLE $50,000 x ARO 0.25 = ALE $12,500 / year
Control quoted: $18,000 / year → costs more than the risk
example.walkthrough: The math does not make the decision alone, but it reframes the conversation: is there a cheaper mitigation, or should leadership formally accept the residual risk? Numbers beat fear.

pitfalls: Common trap: buying insurance instead of fixing the issue — transfer covers financial loss, not the duty to protect data.
Common trap: confusing policies with procedures — a how-to guide with no parent policy has no authority.
Common trap: accepting risk verbally — undocumented acceptance is indistinguishable from negligence later.
Common trap: applying every regulation to every company — scope follows the data you actually hold.
lessons.try_it: Audit a password policy in the Terminal tab →

lessons.title: Security Concepts That Carry the Whole Exam
concepts: The CIA triad is the lens for everything else: confidentiality means only authorized parties can access data (encryption, access controls); integrity means data is accurate and trustworthy (hashing, checksums, digital signatures, change control); availability means systems and data are reachable when needed (redundancy, backups, DDoS mitigation). Exam questions constantly ask which leg a scenario threatens — leaked data is confidentiality, altered data is integrity, an outage is availability.

AAA extends the triad into identity: authentication proves who you are (something you know, have, or are — ideally phishing-resistant), authorization decides what you may do after authenticating (least privilege, role-based access), and accounting logs what you did. Non-repudiation builds on accounting with cryptographic proof — a digital signature — so an actor cannot later deny the action.

Security controls come in flavors you must name precisely. By implementation: technical/logical (firewalls, encryption, MFA), managerial/administrative (policies, risk assessments, training), operational (change management, backup procedures), and physical (locks, badge readers, guards). By purpose: preventive (stop it), detective (find it), corrective (fix it), compensating (alternative when the ideal control is impossible), directive (tell people what to do), and deterrent (discourage attempts).

Threat actors are profiled by motive, capability, and resources. Nation-state/APT groups pursue espionage with custom tooling and extreme patience; organized crime pursues money (ransomware, fraud); hacktivists pursue ideological visibility (defacement, leaks); insiders may be malicious, negligent, or compromised; shadow IT creates unauthorized attack surface; unskilled attackers wield ready-made tools. 'Hacker' is never a sufficient answer — always profile.

Attack vectors are the paths in: phishing (email), smishing (SMS), vishing (voice), spear phishing and whaling (targeted), pretexting (invented scenario), baiting (curiosity lure), tailgating (physical follow-in), watering holes (compromised trusted sites), typosquatting (lookalike domains), and business email compromise (executive/vendor impersonation for fraud). Defense is layered: verification procedures and out-of-band confirmation, phishing-resistant MFA, email authentication (SPF/DKIM/DMARC), and training measured by simulated-phishing click rates — never training alone.

example.code:
# Inspect where a suspicious link REALLY goes before clicking
curl -sIL "https://example-bank-secure.example/login" -o /dev/null -w "final: %{url_effective}\nredirects: %{num_redirects}\n" --max-time 15
dig +short example-bank-secure.example
example.walkthrough: curl -sIL follows the redirect chain silently and reports the effective final URL and redirect count — typosquatted and lookalike domains reveal themselves here because the final domain will not match the brand's real one. dig +short shows the resolving IPs; brand-new or bulletproof-hosted infrastructure is another red flag. Never fetch the body of a suspected phish in a normal browser — headers and DNS give you the verdict safely.

pitfalls: Confusing integrity with confidentiality — leaked data is a confidentiality failure; altered data is an integrity failure
Treating 'hacker' as one actor type — always profile motive, capability, and resources
Assuming training alone stops social engineering — pair it with technical controls like phishing-resistant MFA
Forgetting that non-repudiation needs cryptography (digital signatures), not just logs
lessons.try_it: Take the last three phishing simulations your org ran (or craft three test emails). For each, name the vector (spear phishing, vishing pretext, smishing), the psychological lever (urgency, authority, curiosity), and the one technical control that would have blunted it even if the user clicked.

lessons.title: Know Your Enemy: Malware, Injection, and Network Attacks
concepts: Classify malware by behavior, not by scary name. A virus needs a host file and user action; a worm self-propagates across networks; a trojan disguises itself as legitimate software; a RAT gives remote control; a rootkit provides stealth and persistence (often at kernel or boot level); ransomware encrypts (crypto) or locks (locker) for payment, with double extortion adding a data-leak threat; keyloggers and spyware steal data; logic bombs wait for a trigger; backdoors provide quiet re-entry.

Application attacks exploit trust in input. SQL injection concatenates user input into queries — the definitive fix is parameterized queries (prepared statements). Cross-site scripting comes in reflected, stored, and DOM flavors — fix with context-appropriate output encoding plus input validation. CSRF rides the victim's authenticated session — fix with anti-CSRF tokens and SameSite cookies. Add directory traversal, buffer overflows (bounds checking, ASLR/DEP/NX), race conditions, replay attacks, privilege escalation, and SSRF. A WAF is defense-in-depth, never the primary fix.

Network attacks target the channel. DoS/DDoS spans volumetric floods, protocol attacks, and application-layer abuse — mitigate with CDNs, scrubbing centers, and rate limiting. On-path attacks (ARP poisoning, DNS poisoning, evil twins, rogue APs) are defeated by mutual authentication and encryption. Add deauthentication attacks, RF jamming, and NFC/Bluetooth attacks (bluesnarfing, bluejacking). Encrypt and authenticate the channel: WPA3, TLS, VPN.

Password attacks exploit human reuse. Brute force tries everything; dictionary tries likely words; credential stuffing replays breached username/password pairs; password spraying tries a few common passwords across many accounts to dodge lockouts; rainbow tables precompute hashes (salting defeats them); pass-the-hash reuses the hash itself without cracking. Defenses: MFA (phishing-resistant where it counts), throttling and lockout, breached-password screening, and long unique passwords kept in a manager.

Vulnerability management is a cycle: discover (credentialed scans see configuration and missing patches; non-credentialed scans see what an outsider sees), identify via CVE/NVD, score with CVSS (base = severity, temporal = exploit maturity, environmental = your context), disposition false positives and false negatives, prioritize by risk (exposure + exploitability + asset criticality), then remediate, mitigate, or formally accept. Schedule scans around change windows and always get written authorization first.

example.code:
# Service-version scan of a lab target (get written permission first)
nmap -sV -O -p- --open 192.0.2.10 -oN scan.txt
# Read the essentials from the output
grep -E "^[0-9]+/tcp.*open" scan.txt
example.walkthrough: -sV fingerprints service versions (what is actually listening, not just which ports are open), -O attempts OS detection from TCP/IP stack quirks, -p- --open covers all 65,535 ports but shows only open ones to keep output readable, and -oN saves normal output for your report. The grep pulls the lines that matter for triage: open services with versions to check against CVE/NVD, informing your risk prioritization. Credentialed scans go deeper; this non-credentialed view is what an external attacker sees.

pitfalls: Scanning systems you do not own or lack written permission for — that is unauthorized access
Treating CVSS base score as risk — always add exposure, exploitability, and asset value
Calling everything a 'virus' — worms self-propagate, trojans deceive, ransomware extorts
Relying on a WAF as the fix for injection — fix the code with parameterized queries and encoding
lessons.try_it: Against a lab VM you own, run the nmap service scan above, pick the most exposed service, and look up its CVEs. Write a one-paragraph risk prioritization: CVSS base score, whether an exploit is public, and how exposed the host is.

lessons.title: Building It Secure: Cloud, Zero Trust, and Crypto
concepts: Cloud service models slide the shared-responsibility line. In IaaS the provider secures up to the hypervisor and you own the guest OS upward; in PaaS the provider takes the runtime and you own the app and data; in SaaS the provider owns nearly everything except your data, identities, and configuration. Deployment models (public, private, hybrid, community) change where data lives, not who classifies it. Most cloud breaches are customer misconfiguration, not provider failure — harden identity, storage buckets, and security groups first.

Virtualization concentrates trust in the hypervisor. Type 1 hypervisors run on bare metal; Type 2 run atop a host OS. Threats include VM escape (guest breaks into host), VM sprawl (unmanaged images with stale patches), and snapshot data lingering unencrypted. Containers share the host kernel — lighter than VMs but with weaker isolation — so the host and orchestration plane must be hardened. Secure the virtualization layer first: it is the trust root for everything above it.

Zero Trust (NIST SP 800-207) replaces location-based trust: never trust, always verify. The control plane holds the policy engine and policy administrator (deciding access); the data plane holds policy enforcement points (enforcing it). Principles: assume breach, verify explicitly, least privilege, continuous authentication, and microsegmentation so compromise of one workload does not reach the next. Every connection is authenticated and authorized regardless of where it originates.

Segmentation and resilience make breaches survivable. VLANs, DMZs, and air gaps separate trust zones; jump servers/bastion hosts gate administrative access; firewall types map to layers (stateless packet filters, stateful inspection, NGFW with application awareness, WAF for HTTP, UTM bundles). Resilience: load balancing and clustering for availability, RAID and tested backups (3-2-1, with offline/air-gapped copies that ransomware cannot reach), and hot/warm/cold recovery sites matched to RTO/RPO.

Cryptography essentials: symmetric algorithms (AES-128/256, ChaCha20) use one shared key and are fast for bulk data; asymmetric algorithms (RSA with 2048-bit or larger keys, ECC with 256-bit or larger, Diffie-Hellman) solve key distribution and enable signatures. Hashing (SHA-256/SHA-3) proves integrity — MD5 and SHA-1 are broken for security use; always salt password hashes and stretch them with bcrypt, Argon2, PBKDF2, or scrypt. A digital signature is a hash encrypted with the private key. PKI binds keys to identities: CAs issue, RAs vet, CRLs and OCSP (prefer stapling) handle revocation, and TLS 1.3 brings 1-RTT handshakes, forward secrecy, and the removal of weak ciphers.

example.code:
# Inspect a live TLS endpoint: version, cipher, and chain
openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 -tls1_3 -servername example.com < /dev/null 2>/dev/null | openssl x509 -noout -subject -issuer -dates
echo | openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 2>/dev/null | grep -E "Protocol|Cipher"
example.walkthrough: The first command completes a TLS handshake and pipes the server certificate into openssl x509, printing subject, issuer, and validity dates — expired intermediates and mismatched names show up immediately. The second extracts the negotiated protocol and cipher: you want TLS 1.2 or higher (ideally 1.3) with a forward-secret AEAD cipher, never TLS 1.0/1.1 or RC4/3DES. -servername sends SNI so virtual-hosted sites return the right certificate.

pitfalls: Encrypting without authenticating — encryption alone does not stop tampering; use AEAD ciphers or HMAC
Deploying a certificate without its intermediate chain — clients must chain leaf to root
Using ECB mode or MD5/SHA-1 for security purposes
Assuming the cloud provider secures your data — you own classification, identity, and configuration
lessons.try_it: Run the openssl inspection against three sites you use. Record TLS version, cipher, and days until leaf expiry. Flag anything below TLS 1.2 — then check whether intermediate certificate expirations are monitored anywhere in your organization.

lessons.title: Running the SOC: SIEM, IR, and Forensics
concepts: A SIEM aggregates logs, correlates events, and alerts on patterns no single source reveals. Feed it firewall and IDS/IPS logs, NetFlow, DNS queries, authentication events, and endpoint telemetry. Core use cases: brute-force-then-success, impossible travel, lateral movement, and data exfiltration spikes. Alert fatigue is the enemy — tune rules, baseline normal, and enrich with threat intelligence. SOAR platforms automate enrichment and playbook-driven response on top of the SIEM.

The incident response lifecycle (NIST SP 800-61) has four phases: Preparation (plans, roles, tools, communication trees, tabletop exercises); Detection & Analysis (triage, validation, scoping — is this an event or an incident?); Containment, Eradication & Recovery (stop the spread, remove the cause, restore service); and Post-Incident Activity (lessons learned, control improvements). Tabletop exercises test the plan before a real incident does.

Containment is a judgment call, not a reflex. Network-isolate the host (quarantine VLAN, disable the switch port, host firewall) to stop lateral movement while preserving volatile evidence; powering off destroys memory-resident keys and process artifacts. Disable compromised accounts, revoke sessions and tokens, block malicious indicators at the perimeter — and weigh business continuity at every step. Document each action with timestamps; your notes become the timeline.

Digital forensics follows the order of volatility (RFC 3227): registers and cache, memory, network state, running processes, disk, remote logs, physical configuration, archival media — most ephemeral first. Image disks through write blockers, hash everything with SHA-256 at acquisition and verify at every transfer, and maintain an unbroken chain of custody: who handled what, when. Issue a legal hold early so nobody deletes evidence. Correlate timelines across endpoint, network, and identity logs — one source rarely tells the story.

Log analysis is the analyst's daily craft. Learn syslog severity levels; Windows Event IDs 4624 (successful logon), 4625 (failed logon), and 4688 (process creation); Linux auth.log for SSH brute force; NetFlow for beaconing and exfiltration volume; DNS logs for tunneling and DGAs. Baseline normal first — you cannot spot abnormal without it. When hunting, pivot: IP to user to host to process, across sources, until the story is complete.

example.code:
# Hunt brute-force logins: top source IPs by failed-password count
grep "Failed password" /var/log/auth.log | awk '{print $(NF-3)}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -nr | head -10
# Then check whether any of those IPs later succeeded
grep "Accepted password" /var/log/auth.log | awk '{print $(NF-3)}' | sort -u
example.walkthrough: The first pipeline filters failed-password lines, extracts the source IP field, and counts occurrences per IP — a sudden spike from one IP is your brute-force or password-spraying indicator. The second lists every IP with a successful login; any IP appearing in both lists is a failures-then-success compromise candidate — exactly the SIEM correlation from the scenarios, done by hand. Cross-reference with GeoIP and your VPN logs before escalating.

pitfalls: Powering off a compromised host before capturing memory — respect the order of volatility
Treating every SIEM alert as an incident — triage: validate, then escalate
Doing forensics without hashing and chain of custody — technically interesting, legally useless
Analyzing one log source in isolation — correlate across endpoint, network, and identity
lessons.try_it: On a Linux lab box, generate 20 failed SSH logins from another host, then run the pipeline above. Tune it: add a threshold (e.g., flag IPs with more than 10 failures) and write offenders to a blocklist file with timestamps.

lessons.title: Running Security as a Program: Risk, Frameworks, Privacy
concepts: Risk management turns fear into math and decisions. Risk is likelihood times impact. Qualitative analysis ranks risks on a matrix (low/medium/high); quantitative analysis computes ALE = SLE x ARO, where SLE is asset value times exposure factor. The risk register tracks each risk with an owner; treatment options are accept (document and sign off), avoid (eliminate the activity), mitigate (reduce likelihood or impact), and transfer (insurance, outsourcing). Whatever remains is residual risk, measured against leadership's risk appetite and tolerance.

NIST CSF 2.0 organizes programs into six functions: Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover. Around it: the NIST Risk Management Framework for authorizing systems, SP 800-53's control catalog, SP 800-61 for incident response, and SP 800-207 for Zero Trust. Frameworks organize controls and create a common language — they do not replace judgment about your specific risks.

Industry frameworks overlap heavily — map once, satisfy many. ISO/IEC 27001 defines ISMS requirements (and certification), 27002 gives control guidance; PCI DSS protects cardholder data; SOC 2 reports on service-organization controls; CIS Controls prioritize safeguards into implementation groups IG1–IG3; COBIT governs IT overall. Start from your obligations (contracts, regulators, customers) and map controls to all of them.

Controls need two taxonomies. By implementation: managerial (policies, risk assessments, training), technical (encryption, MFA, firewalls), operational (change management, media handling, personnel security), physical (badge access, cameras, guards). By purpose: preventive, detective, corrective, deterrent, compensating, directive. Policies sit at the top but are not executable alone — they need standards (mandatory rules), procedures (step-by-step), and guidelines (recommended practice) beneath them.

Privacy and data governance decide what you may collect and keep. Classify data (public, internal, confidential, restricted) and attach handling rules to each class. Know PII and PHI; practice data minimization and purpose limitation; define retention schedules and destroy properly (crypto-shredding, degaussing, physical destruction). DLP enforces handling rules technically. Breach notification duties (GDPR's 72 hours, state laws) start the clock at discovery — which is why detection maturity is a privacy control too.

example.walkthrough: This one-liner encodes ALE = SLE x ARO twice — expected annual loss before and after the control — then compares the savings to the control's annualized cost. The verdict rule is the whole discipline of quantitative risk: buy controls whose risk reduction exceeds their cost. Remember the limits: SLE and ARO are estimates, and qualitative factors (regulatory mandates, reputation) can override the math.

pitfalls: Mixing SLE (per-incident) with ALE (annualized) in cost comparisons
Treating risk acceptance as 'do nothing' — it requires documentation and sign-off
Assuming one framework covers all obligations — map each data type and jurisdiction
Writing policies nobody can execute — pair every policy with standards and procedures
lessons.try_it: Pick one real risk in your environment. Estimate SLE and ARO, compute ALE, price one control, and run the verdict. Then write the two-sentence risk-acceptance memo you would file if the math says skip.

Interview/exam power: when asked 'how does X work?', narrate the journey — 'it starts here, then...'. This demonstrates senior-level systems thinking

TRIGGER event occurs

  → State changes propagate (follow the ripple)
  → Final outcome delivered

Each arrow is a living handoff, not a static box.
example.walkthrough: This is the 'jet engine cutaway' for your field: instead of memorizing isolated facts, you see the entire flow as a moving sequence. Practice narrating this journey out loud.

pitfalls: Memorizing terms without understanding the processes they participate in
Drawing architecture diagrams as boxes without showing the data flow between them
Answering 'how does X work?' with a definition instead of walking through the sequence

lessons.title: How to Use This Bootcamp
concepts: The study order is deliberate — follow it: Start Here first, then work each domain in listed order. Domains unlock as you demonstrate mastery, because SY0-701 topics build on each other.
What 'terminal' means: the Terminal tab is a real shell where labs run. Every lab command executes there — you learn by doing, not by reading about doing.
Lessons teach concepts with a worked example, pitfalls, and a try-it prompt. Scenarios test judgment under realistic pressure. Labs prove you can execute. The mock assessment ties it all together.
Knowledge checks verify understanding before a lesson counts complete — you cannot click through. Spaced repetition resurfaces weak areas automatically.
Your progress syncs as you work. A domain is mastered when lessons are verified, scenarios answered, and labs completed.

example.code:
Day 1: complete all 4 Start Here lessons
Day 2-3: first two content domains (lessons + scenarios)
Day 4+: one domain per day, labs each evening
Final 3 days: mock assessment runs + capstone build
example.walkthrough: This order exists because later domains assume earlier vocabulary. Skipping ahead creates gaps that the mock assessment will expose — painfully. Trust the sequence.
